maintopic: FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENT BETWEEN BRITISH GOVERNMENT AND C.P.R.

speechtext:
Hon. Sir THOMAS WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 47, to facilitate certain financial arrangements between the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and for other purposes.
He said: The object of the Bill is indicated in the title which I have just read. I may explain further, for the information of the House, that the Government of the United Kingdom, for the purpose of making financial provision for the prosecution of the war. has taken over and acquired, and proposes to take over or acquire, by compulsory purchase or otherwise, from persons resident in the United Kingdom, certain securities of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and of the companies whose lines are leased to that company. The purpose of the British Government in so taking over these securities is to make them available for raising money on this side of the Atlantic; in other words, to assist the exchange situation, which for a considerable time has been adverse to Great Britain. In order that the British Government may have securities which can be sold on this side of the Atlantic, they have requested the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to issue collateral trust bonds of the company payable in United States currency. These collateral trust bonds are to be exchanged by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, if and when requested by the Government of the United Kingdom, for the consolidated debenture stock and other securities payable in sterling which shall have been acquired by the Government of the United Kingdom in London. That, in brief, is the transaction, and it is in order to empower the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to issue these collateral trust bonds to an amount sufficient for the purpose of exchange with the British Government for these consolidated debenture and other sterling securities that this. Bill is introduced.

maintopic: FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENT BETWEEN BRITISH GOVERNMENT AND C.P.R.
speechtext: As I understand the Bill as outlined by my hon. friend, it contemplates not to add to the liabilities of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, but simply to substitute one class of security for another?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENT BETWEEN BRITISH GOVERNMENT AND C.P.R.
speechtext: That is the object of the Bill. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has asked that the Bill be introduced in order to facilitate arrangements which it has been specifically requested by the Imperial Government to enter into.

maintopic: FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENT BETWEEN BRITISH GOVERNMENT AND C.P.R.
speechtext:
I am under the impression that in the report of the proceedings of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company the president is reported as having stated that, owing to the entry of the United States into the war and the loan to Great Britain by the United States of $7,000,000,000, the carrying out of the proposal as originally made was not now contemplated. Perhaps my hon. friend will be able to inform the House whether or not that is so.

Of course, if it is so, it would not be necessary to proceed further with this proposed measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENT BETWEEN BRITISH GOVERNMENT AND C.P.R.
speechtext:
When I first
placed this Bill upon the Order Paper the matter was quite urgent, because an issue of these bonds was about to be made in New York. On account of the financial situation which developed by reason of the entry of the United States into the war, it was found inadvisable to proceed. No such issue is now in immediate contemplation, but I know that the British Government has asked the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to proceed with this legislation in order that it may be available if required.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.	-

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MR. J. D. TAYLOR.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MR. J. D. TAYLOR.
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege and to call attention to an unusual episode which occurred during the debate in this House on the 1st of May., the speaker being the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Levi Thomson), who is reported in Hansard, page 1021, as follows:
I would not like to charge any man with disloyalty, not even those political colonels who strut around our country in the King's uniform, drawing big pay, and who have been on a free trip across the Atlantic to England or France, but who, the moment they smelt gunpowder, turned tail and skipped back home, leaving their men to go to the front without them.
If the audience to whom this is addressed, that is, the Canadian public,- had been present in the chamber and could have visualized the scene, it would not have heen necessary to make any remarks in answer to the hon. gentleman; but unfortunately, such is not the case, and his remarks, going to a public uninformed as to the source of a statement of this kind, are very mischievous and insulting to the commanding officers m Hie Majesty's army, of whom 1 have the honour to be one. I am sure, Sir, you will Tecognize that this statement is doubly out of order; in the first place as a flagrant breach of Rule 19 of this House, and in the next as a breach of that most particular rule of parliamentary debate which prohibits any reflection on the honour of officers of the naval or military

forces'. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle has not been present in the chamber since I arrived from British Columbia a week ago. but on a later occasion, when he is present, I purpose, with the permission of the House, making a motion which I think will he in order, namely: that that hon. member be ordered to withdraw these remarks and that they be expunged from the Hansard for the day named.
In the meantime, however, I think I am in order in making a personal explanation- at least personal to myself-as to how I, one of these political colonels, who no doubt was referred to (because the passage is meaningless if it does not refer to colonels who are members of the House of Commons) come to be here to-day.
I may say that I had as clear an understanding with the Department of Militia in this country .as any commanding officer could have, that I was raising a battalion with which I would serve at the front so long as the battalion served. As I have said in the House before, I recognized that military exigencies, when we arrived in England, made it seem necessary to break up the .battalion and to remove, not the commanding officer from the battalion, but the battalion from the commanding officer, which is the real process there. The brigadier in a case like that takes command of the whole battalion, calls out the officers, directs his sergeant-major to march away the men in accordance with the notice already given that those men are to be attached to a reserve battalion to go forward as drafts, and the commanding officer is left to wind up the affairs of the battalion. That is what occurred to me and to several other members of Parliament in command of battalions who arrived in England at the same time as I did. Subsequently we received, through military headquarters, a specific invitation from the Government of Canada to return to Canada to attend to our parliamentary duties. When that invitation was extended to me I replied in writing that I would be pleased to accept it provided that I was not required for military service. The rejoinder to that was information to me that my passage had been booked on a .steamer sailing a couple of days after I received the notice, and I think the same explanation applies to every other of those so-called political colonels. May I suggest, in conclusion, that if we desire to have His Majesty's uniform respected in Canada, by the people of Canada, it would not be out of place for the House of Commons to give the lead.
On the Orders of the Day:

I had not (he pleasure of being present in the House on the 11th instant when my right hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and acting leader of the Government (Sir George Foster) made a statement with regard to the building of ships, in particular, of wooden vessels, a matter which is of very great importance and which is exciting a great deal of interest, more especially in the Maritime Provinces. My right hon. friend is reported to have made this statement:
As to wooden ships, an arrangement is now completed and is being carried out whereby any body or any company that can undertake in a bona fide way to build wooden ships and to deliver them within a certain time, will get the opportunity of building the ships and will be assured that the ship will pay for the cost of construction, with a reasonable profit.
It would be desirable in the public interest that certain details, which are wanting in the observations of my right hon. friend, should be given to the House and to the country. As my right hon. friend is aware, there are in New Brunswick a large number of places, for instance, in the city of St. John, and ait other points along the St. John river, the Kennebecasis, the Mirami-chi, the Restigouche, and other points in the counties of Kent and Gloucester where in former days wooden shipbuilding was carried on very extensively, and where there are admirable sites for the building of ships. 1 think the only thing that is wanting is that definite information should be given to people who are interested as to the terms upon which contracts would be let and as to the standard of vessels which would be required, in order to induce quite a large number of persons to engage in wooden ship building. At present they have no information upon the subject; they do not know to whom to apply; they do not know the standard of vessels required, and it is desirable that such information should be made public. My object in bringing this matter to the attention of the House and particularly to the attention of my right hon. friend is that that information should be furnished as early as possible.

It is not an unreasonable demand that proper publicity should be given in relation to the question
which has been brought up by my hon. friend. In the first place I may say that inquiries addressed to the Munitions Board will bring all the information of the kind hinted at by my hon. friend. In the second place if it should seem advisable to make an announcement to the public in a fuller ox perhaps a more speedy way the Government. will confer with the Munitions Board as to such an announcement.

I would presume that in a matter of this importance there must have been correspondence between the Imperial authorities and the Dominion Government. Perhaps the best way of making the announcement would be to bring down the correspondence.

Such correspondence would foe between the British Government and the Imperial Munitions Board, which is entirely under the British Government. If any correspondence in reference to this matter has passed between the British and Dominion Governments, that of course could be brought down.

One would not suppose that correspondence is taking place between the Imperial Government and the Munitions Board, of which this Government have no knowledge whatever; it would not pass over the head of this Government.

Bless the heart of my right hon. friend! Surely he does not adhere to the position that the British Government either through an agent or otherwise cannot make a purchase or close a contract in this country without coming to the Dominion Government.

Bless my
heart to this extent:	the British Government can, but I do not suppose that they do-

They would
bother this Government to death if we were consulted every time.

I dare say
they have done so, and that is why I want the correspondence.

QUESTION AS TO AID BY CANADIAN GOVERNMENT.	.
On the Orders of the Day:

Has the Government given any aid either by loan of money or otherwise to the Im-

perial Munitions Board for the building of wooden ships in Canada?
I have given all the information on that head that it is possible to give. If my hon. friend requires the specific information he has detailed today, I will see how far his wishes can be met.

My hon. friend stated in his remarks on the 11th instant that ships were being built in Canada and that every available shipyard was being utilized. I beg to differ from my hon. friend because I know of a number of shipyards where absolutely no work is being done. Would the minister be good enough to state to the House at an early date where shipbuilding is being carried on under the arrangement he has spoken of?

It is not the
first time my hon. friend has differed from me, and found himself in the wrong in the end. I will try and get him all the information for which his ardent soul so longs.
It is a reasonable soul too.
On the Orders of the Day:

Has the Minister of Labour any further information regarding the coal mining camps in the West? I read in the Montreal Gazette this morning that the District Union has called out the miners in all the camps in Alberta and Eastern British Columbia. The United Mine Workers of America control all the coal mining camps in Southern Alberta and Eastern British Columbia, and if this report is true the mines will all be closed and there will probably be a shortage of coal, because I do not think there is any coal stored in the West at the present time. It is also stated in the despatch that the Minister of labour has suggested a Royal Commission, and that the parties are considering it. The coal mining situation in the West is very serious, and I should like tp know just what the Government is doing. The minister might also state whether a communication has been received from the operators in regard to keeping open the mines and operating them; I saw a telegram to that effect in a western paper the other day. I would also remind the minister of what purported to be an .official statement from the Government in the latter part of

January last when this trouble began. A proposition was supposed to come from the Government that if the difficulties between the men and the operators could not be settled, the Government would take over the mines and operate them for the benefit of the people. I should like to know whether this is correct, and what action the Government purposes taking.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour):
speechtext: The representatives of the miners were in session in Calgary some five or six weeks, negotiating a new agreement. They finally came to an agreement, subject to ratification by the miners. It seems there is a certain provision in the constitution of the United Mine Workers of America whereby their representatives can only make a tentative agreement which becomes final on ratification by the miners. In this case the agreement was rejected by The miners by a large majority. The representatives of the miners then called a meeting of the local lodges to be held in Calgary last Thursday night, to decide what action should be taken, and so far as my dnfprma-tion goes they have not yet reached a conclusion. I sent a message to the president of the organization on Saturday night, but have not yet received a reply, so I am not in a position to say what course they intended to take.

maintopic: SHORTAGE OF SALT FOR FISH CURING.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: SHORTAGE OF SALT FOR FISH CURING.
speechtext:
I desire to refer for a moment to the question that was brought up the other day by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) as to what arrangements the Government are making for securing tonnage for the transportation of salt from Mediterranean ports to ports in the Maritime Provinces. A serious condition is likely to prevail in the Maritime Provinces shortly on account of lack of the salt which is required in the fish business. In the Maritime Provinces 15,000 or 20,000 pounds of salt are required annually in the fish business, and it looks at the moment as if there will be great difficulty in securing the necessary supply. I would point out that Admiralty transports are frequently arriving at Halifax from Mediterranean ports without cargo. Many of them arrive with mud ballast, which must cost the ship money to load and unload. Many of these ships have been offered as high as 35 shillings a ton to bring salt to the maritime ports, but they have declined to do so.
It happened just recently that a ship left the Mediterranean in ballast, having passed quite close to a port where a cargo of salt might have been procured. The situation is extremely grave in the Maritime Provinces, for the reasons I have given. It seems to me that the matter is not being fairly dealt with by the Admiralty, or by some person who should exercise authority. There would seem to be no reason why ships coming from Mediterranean ports to the Maritime Provinces in ballast should not carry salt for which they receive very favourable freight rates indeed. I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) will be seized of the importance of the matter and will do everything possible to secure ships to carry salt.

speakeroldname: Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: SHORTAGE OF SALT FOR FISH CURING.
speechtext:
Everything that can possibly be done from this side has been done with that object in view. The authorities at home are fully seized of the necessities of this side, and the transport
authorities are quite willing that vessels should bring salt to their ports of destination. But they can not be expected to waste too much time going distances in order to reach the points to which the salt is consigned. That is the only difficulty that intervened. The matter has been thoroughly represented; the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) while in London has taken the matter up with the authorities themselves, and I have information that they are perfectly accordant with the idea and will in every case carry it out. There may be some difficulty with regard to freight rates, I do not know about that; but I imagine they are not unreasonable in the freights they charge.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC BRANCH LINES COMPANY.

speechtext:
House in Committee on Bill No. 41-Mr. ^-Blain in the Chair-respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company-Mr. J. A. Currie.
On secfion 2-extension of time for completion of certain authorized railways:

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC BRANCH LINES COMPANY.
speechtext:
I am very
pleased to see in the House my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie), who is in charge of this Bill and who takes an interest in the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. These lines mentioned in the Bill are intended to be feeders of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Is my hon. friend aware that at the present time the Government are dismantling the Grand Trunk Pacific and destroying it east and west? Since my hon. friend takes an interest in the road, I hope he will see that the Government do not carry any further their nefarious operations, but keep up the railway. Otherwise these branches if built will be of no use.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC BRANCH LINES COMPANY.
speechtext:
As this Bill, if passed,
will very largely affect the railway situation as reported on by the Royal Commission appointed some time ago to investigate the whole railway and transportation situation in Canada, I think we should know from the minister whether or not he has considered the majority and the minority reports made by the Royal Commission, and if he is prepared to inform the House whether or not he will advise the adoption of either of those reports; and if not what the Government propose to do in connection with the railway situation in Canada, which is certainly in a very serious condition, to my mind a very dangerous condition, in relation to the beat interests of Canada. I think that, at least before this Bill is read the third time, we should hear from the minister the policy of the Government, as this Bill gives the Grand Trunk Pacific Company further large powers for building branch lines, many of which will come directly into competition with branch lines of the Canadian Northern in that locality. The majority of the Royal Commission recommend that the Government should acquire both of those railway systems and thereby do away with the necessity of duplicating these branch lines. Before anything further is done in regard to the 'construction of branch lines, I think we should know what views the Government have, if they have yet arrived at a conclusion in the matter, and what is likely to 'be done to alleviate the very serious railway situation in Canada.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC BRANCH LINES COMPANY.
speechtext:
I beg to say that I
have read both the majority and the minority reports, and an announcement will be made in the House very shortly of what we propose to do.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC BRANCH LINES COMPANY.
speechtext:
I was asked to take charge of this Bill, having had charge of some of these Bills before for the Grand Trunk Railway. I recognize the force of the remarks of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). At the same time, as the Government are going to bring down a policy on the railway situation
4 p.m. very shortly, I hardly think that policy should be discussed in connection with this Bill. So far as I know, no action is going to be taken by the Government.- These charters are expiring and this company comes to this honourable House and asks the House to renew them. A large sum of money is involved even in the passing of this Bill. I am well aware that the roads referred to here are perhaps not in as good a position financially as they might be. All of these matters, however, are questions beyond the scope of this Bill, and all I can do is to ask the House to pass the Bill, Should the Government see fit to take over the road before this Bill reaches its third reading, I am satisfied the House will remit the fees to the Grand Trunk Company, and that no further action will be taken. All I can do as promoter of the Bill is to forward it in good faith to the company that asks ns to renew it.
Sir WULFRID LAURIER-: I did not make these remarks with any view of opposing

the Bill; on the contrary, I am quite in sympathy with it, and with the building of branch lines of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. I still believe it is a good enterprise. What I had in mind was to enlist the sympathy of my hon. friend, who is a supporter of the Government, and to ask him to see that they did not dismantle and destroy that property which he is now asking us to make better and more useful. My hon. friend is aware that in the East the Grand Trunk Pacific railway has been largely damaged and destroyed. The grades have been destroyed, and now the rails are being taken up from the sidings. In the W est the rails are being taken up from the main line. If the road is further subjected to this process of destruction, it will not have the same value. Therefore it is that I urge on my hon. friend to do all in his power to prevent that process going any further, and to see that the Government keep the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway going. I hope that my appeal has not fallen on deaf ears.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should introduce legislation at this Session which will extend the franchise to every British citizen who enlisted with the Canadian Forces for Overseas Service, and who was a resident of Canada at the time of enlistment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, matters relating to suffrage are always of considerable in-

terest, not only to Parliament, but to the country generally. Some one 'has said that the destruction or salvation of states depends upon the matter of regulating the suffrage. For that reason I think it very important at this time to have the matter discussed and dealt with by this House which is referred to in the resolution I have the honour of proposing. The main object of this resolution is to grant the suffrage to all soldiers who are under twenty-one years of age, and thus to put them on a parity with all others who are fighting for our country. From the days of ancient Greece and Rome, when suffrage was first introduced, there has been .a gradual extension of the privilege, being at first very restricted, but gradually growing wider and wider as the years have passed. All countries, however, still have their restrictions on suffrage. For instance, every country requires that the voter shall be a subject or citizen of the country in which he votes. Also, that every voter shall be a resident of the country. Many countries still retain the property qualification, limiting the suffrage to those citizens who possess a certain amount of property. All countries, I think, have an age qualification, although this varies much in the different countries. In Denmark the age at which one is first allowed to vote is 30 years; in Belgium, Japan and Norway, 25 years; Austria, 24 years; Hungary, 20 years. I think that in all other countries the age is fixed at 21 years. Other requirements are provided in various countries. Some countries, for instance, require that the voter shall be able to read and write. In some countries-and strangely, I think, although probably there is good reason for it, in three of our allies, Russia, Italy and France-soldiers are not allowed to vote at all, unless the law has been changed since the outbreak of the (present war.
In general terms, granting the suffrage to any person presupposes that that person is possessed of sufficient intelligence to be aoie to give a vote which will be for the benefit of the country, and that he will bring sufficient knowledge and intelligence to bear on the process of voting to enable him to do that which is best for the country. It also presupposes that .the voter has sufficient interest in his country's affairs to be willing to cast his vote and to cast it in a way in which he, at least, believes to be in the best interest of that country.
It seems to me, however, that while all these qualifications may serve a good purpose, and while some of them may be abso-
[Mr. Steeled
lutely essential, at this day -there is a higher qualification which has been established by the present war, and that qualification is the ability and willingness to give service to the state. I believe, that we in Canada especially should add that qualification to the others which we have m force and that the suffrage should be granted to many c: those who have shown their willingness and ability to serve the state, and especially those who are in our army to-day and are giving us such splendid service. It was these young men under twenty-one years of age, who at present by our Franchise Act are deprived of the privilege of voting, that I had specially in mind when introducing this resolution. The Soldiers' Voting Bill, passed in 1915, has this for its first clause:
Every male British subject of twenty-one years of age or upwards serving in the military forces of Canada in the present war (hereinafter called "volunteer"), who, within six months immediately preceding the date when he was appointed to or enlisted in such forces, had been resident in any electoral district in Canada for a period of not less than thirty days, shall be entitled to vote in the electoral district in which he was last so resident in the manner hereinafter set out, notwithstanding his absence from such electoral district or from Canada: Provided that if any person was, at the time he was so appointed or enlisted, qualified to vote in any other electoral district in Canada, he shall vote in such other district only.
You will note that in that clause several restrictions which apply to other voters have been removed in- the case of the soldier. For instance, the soldier who is twenty-one years of age or upwards may vote even though he is absent from the country, which the civilian is not allowed to do. He may vote notwithstanding that he has no fixed residence at the time of enlistment, and no civilian is -allowed this privilege. So we see, by the Soldiers' Voting Bill -some of those in the army were given special privileges which those not in the army do not enjoy. So, when I ask by this resolution that the franchise -shall be extended to include others in the army, I am not proposing anything that is so very radical.
In 1915, there were few who thought that the needs of the war would be so great as they have proven to be. At that time, judging by the discussion in this House, it was generally thought that if Canada supplied
50.000	men she would not require to supply more. No person, I think I may safely say, thought that within two and a half years Canada would have am army of over
400.000	men. When we have such a large number enrolled in the overseas forces, it

means that there is a correspondingly large number of young men under twenty-one who are giving the best service to this country that it is possible to give, yet who are denied the privilege of taking part in the affaire of this country when they return home, or when an election shall come on. Among those who are twenty-one years of age, I think I may safely say, are some of the best boys Canada has produced. And not only that but I think I can well say that, accordingly to the view of our people, the Canadian boys under twenty-one years of age are equal in intelligence and ability to the young men of any other counry in the world. Amongst these are several thousand students from,,, our colleges and universities, young men who cannot be said not to possess sufficient intelligence to be able to vote, or young men who take so little interest in the affairs of their country as to be disqualified from voting. I believe that these young men have all the qualifications, intellectual and other, that are required to make them voters of the very first class.
When the call came in 1914 for men to serve our country, there was no question then regarding the ability of boys under 21 years of age to serve. When the call came for men to protect our country, our homes our property and our lives, and to maintain the integrity of the British Empire and preserve the freedom of Canada, no person would stand up and say: We can not accept the services of any man under 21 years of age. Why should we apply that rule after they have fought and endured, and yea, sacrificed even their lives? Why should we apply that rule, after these men under 21 years of age have done such splendid service for their country, why should we say to them: You can have no further active participation in the affairs of this country. Many of them will not return, many of them will leave their bodies on Flanders fields, but large numbers will return to this country, large numbers will be residents of Canada, large numbers will be residents of the various electoral districts, every one of them will be British subjects, and how can we say to them: We are quite willing that you should fight for our land, we are quite willing that you should face the enemy, we admire what you have done at St. Julien, Courcelette, and Vimy Ridge, we give you all honour for your splendid services in France and on the continent of Europe, but we can not see our way clear to granting you the right and the privilege
of marking the ballot when you return to Canada until you have become a year, or two years, or three years, older and until you have convinced us that you possess sufficient intelligence to mark that ballot properly. Is that the treatment that we are going to give these splendid boys to whom we are so deeply indebted when they return? I can not believe it is. These young men have assisted in making a new Canada. They have assisted in preserving the freedom of the institutions of Canada but they have also done splendid service in creating a nation that is going to be a new Canada. We are looking forward to greater opportunities and privileges among the nations of the world and we are looking forward to being a Canada with a history of sacrifice and heroism that will be a source of pride to our people for generations to come That Canada is possible partly as the result, at least, of the exertions, the efforts and heroism of the boys fighting in France today who are under 21 years of age, and this Parliament should not, say to these boys: We are indebted to you for the service you have performed there but we can not extend to you the rights of citizenship when you return home.
The next Parliament of Canada will have largely to deal with problems and questions which have been created by this war. It would be only fair and right that the men who have created the conditions which that Parliament will have to deal with should have the right to say who shall be the representatives of the Canadian people in the Parliament which has to deal with these problems which they, by their splendid efforts, have created. I think we should not say to these young men that we are willing that they should direct the bullets intended to destroy the enemy but we are unwilling that they should mark their ballots which will be the instruments by which the welfare of Canada shall be maintained for the next few years at least. Each man who has fought should have the right to say how the fruits of his efforts are going to be dealt with. For that reason I hope that this resolution will be passed and that the franchise will be extended to these young men. I believe they will exercise their franchise with at least as much intelligence as the average elector in the country, that they will exercise it with as deep an interest in the affairs of the country as the average elector will, and I would feel disposed to go further and say that they will be amongst the most intelligent and

the most interested young Canadians that we will have in this country.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
I have listened with great interest to the remarks on this resolution that have fallen from the lips of the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele). I am glad to have the opportunity of saying a few brief words in support of the resolution, which I trust will commend itself to the House. In round numbers, probably 400,000 of the men of Canada have enlisted for active service overseas. A considerable percentage of this number is possibly composed of young men under the age of 21 years, who, therefore, are not entitled to vote. Many of these young men, some to my personal knowledge, had taken an active part in all matters relating to the welfare of Canada previous to their enlistment. In regard to their loyalty, there can be no question. The way in which they rushed to enlist at the beginning of the war makes it clear that every one of them is intensely loyal. Many have returned to this country maimed and wounded, many have laid down their lives, and many more to-day are fighting out battles in France. It seems to me that if there is any one class in this country who are entitled to a special right to be consulted, and to express their views on the affairs of this country at the present time, it is these young men who so willingly volunteered, and were ready to lay down their lives for their country. More particularly, it seems to me, at a time when we are confronted by great war problems-and after the war these problems will be even more difficult than they are now-should these valiant young patriots have s.ome voice in the settlement of these questions. 'If they are old enough to fight, and if they -are old enough, if need be, to die for their country, they are old enough to vote. These young men have matured, not by age, not by years, tout by hard and bitter experience; and I think it wpuld toe a hardship of -the worst kind not to allow them the right to exercise their franchise when they return to Canada.
The resolution as introduced by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) includes all men of British birth who have enlisted for pveTseas service, and this, of course, includes the Indians in this country, who have again shown their loyalty by enlisting in large numbers from all parts of this Dominion. From the reserve of the Six Nations, in the county I ' represent, some 400 young Indians haye enlisted. One fMr. Steele. 1
of the first from the county of Brant to lay down his life for his country was a young Indian, Lieutenant Cameron Brant, a member of the 114th Regiment, and a direct de-seenident of the Great Indian chief, Joseph Brant, after whom the city of Brantford and the county of Brant are named. As you are aware, none of these Indians are now entitled to the franchise, and it seems to me that it>
would be a mere act of justice. that those at least who have enlisted should be allowed the right to vote. But I would go further than this; I would say that the Government should, at a very early date, take into their earnest and serious consideration the matter of restoring the franchise to the Indians of this country, the franchise which was given to them by a former Conservative Government and which was taken- from them toy the late Administration for, possibly, some reason, but for what good reason I cannot imagine. I do know this, that there are no similar number of white men in this country or in. any other country who would exercise the franchise more intelligently or more honestly than the Indians of the Six Nations reserve, and I believe~ that what I say in regard to the Indians of the Six Nations will apply also to the Indians of all other reserves in this country. I should toe very glad to know that the full franchise was to be restored to them. But, in any case, I trust that the franchise will at least be given to those who have enlisted- I should like in this connection to apply to these brave young Indians who have gone forth to battle for the Empire, the words of the late gifted Indian poetess, Pauline Johnson, herself one of the Six JNations. In a poem composed by Pauline Johnson, the following words occur:
Few of them have the blood of kings,
And few are of courtly birth,
But none are vagabonds or rogues,-Of doubtful race and worth.
And each has one credential,
Which enables him to brag,
He fought for right and Canada,
And upheld the British Flag.
I should be remiss in my duty if I did not say a word in regard to the splendid work that has been done along patriotic lines by the Indian women on the reserve.
I would simply say, in a word, that the work they have done has not been surpassed in any part of this Dom-5 p.m. inion, and I trust- that whqn woman suffrage comes, as I have no doubt it will come, the Indian women on the Reserve will be accorded

equal rights with their white sisters. They are well deserving of it, and I believe they will exercise the franchise just as well as the white women could or will. I am quite sure that this resolution of the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) will commend itself to the members of this House, and I also feel quite sure that the Government will give it their very earnest and careful consideration.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
Mr-Speaker, I should like, in a word, to put myself on record as being very heartily in favour of the resolution before the House. The qualification for voting in Federal affairs is that of manhood suffrage. We have an arbitrary method of defining the time at which a male reaches the point of manhood. I do not think that any of us would seek ito apply that artificial method to the men who have gone to the front and say that there are men in the trenches from Canada who have not reached the age of manhood. I do not think that any one would deny the possession of manhood to every man who hae voluntarily gone to fight for Canada at the front. So that if manhood suffrage be our test of the right to exercise the franchise, we certainly have men who, although they are not twenty-one years of age, have lived amply up to that qualification. I have not the slightest hesitation in giving adherence to the resolution, and I support it most heartily.
Mr. GEORGE A. ELLIOTT (Middlesex North):	Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with
the hon. member from North Brant (Mr. Fisher), and also the hon. member from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) in. saying a few words of appreciation of the resolution introduced in this House by the hon. member from South Perth (Mr. Steele). I appreciate the meaning of the resolution more fully than I have words to express. When we take into consideration the fact that over 400,000 of Canada's sons have responded to the call for service for our King and country, and that many of them are under the age of twenty-one, we realize that these men, though under twenty-one years of age, should be entitled to the same privileges as other citizens of our land. When the British Government and the Canadian Government appealed to their subjects throughout the Empire and asked for volunteers, they called for men between the ages of eighteen and forty-five years; they fixed the minimum age at eighteen years. No doubt, the authorities felt that many a
young man under 21 throughout the Empire was just as fit physically and mentally to be a soldier as wene older men. I believe that fully one-third of the men who enlisted in the Middlesex regiment from my county and who have gone overseas, are under twenty-one years of age. Many of our young men, as has been stated by previous speakers, have made the supreme, the greatest possible sacrifice. Some of them will never return to the land from which they went. I could, if I so wished, mention several mothers in the community in which I live who are to-day mourning the loss of their sons, many of them under twenty-one years of age. I remember well, during August of last year when our home regiment was leaving our county, that a great many people gathered at the station to bid our boys farewell. I can see at this moment the anxiety shown by those mothers and parents on behalf of their sons. I can also see them bidding their sons good bye-some of them for the last time-and sending them away with their good wishes and their prayers. I listened the other day with a great deal of regret to the remarks made by two or three members of the Opposition, in which they attempted to reflect upon the character and habits of those young men while in England and France. During the six years that I have had the honour of being in this Parliament, I have never appreciated anything more than the words of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) when he said, a few days ago, that it was not for us as Canadian citizens who had stayed at home to dictate for a moment as as to what our boys should do. Would any member of the Opposition-indeed, any man in this House or out of it- dare to say to the mothers who'had sent their boys of eighteen overseas-boys who had gone voluntarily; boys who had the spirit to go and fight for their fcountry-that these young men were not entitled to the privileges which other men of Canada have?
I wish to say a word-I was glad that the member for Brant (Mr. Fisher) mentioned it-regarding the Indians of my county. In the county of Middlesex we have a number of Indians, many of whom were among the first to respond to the call for service overseas and a number of whom have laid down their lives for their country. For a number of years those men have not had the privilege of the franchise such as the rest of us enjoy. They are an intelligent race of Indians, having their schools and their institutes. They are capable; they

are good business men. An indication of their worth and their efficiency is found in the fact that although our reserve is a small one, nearly 100 of them have joined the colours and have gone overseas. I do think that those men should have the privilege of a franchise; I do think that they deserve it. We have in Canada many foreigners of all nationalities who really do not know anything about Canadian affairs or Canadian institutions and who, in a sense, are not helping to build Canada up or to make it great.	They have not
contributed to any extent to the different patriotic funds, nor yet have they enlisted. Yet these men, after they have lived in this country a certain length of time, are allowed to vote. Under the present Franchise Act our young men under 21 years of age cannot vote. Let me say, in conclusion., that I am perfectly in sympathy with this resolution. I believe that every man who has a uniform on, and is serving his country, though he be a boy in years, is entitled to the same privileges which the rest of us enjoy.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
I am sure that the hon. member for Bonaventure (Hon. Charles Marcil) must feel extremely gratified because of the very strong expressions which have fallen from the lips of hon. gentlemen opposite this afternoon in reference to the extension of the franchise to all our .soldier boys. The House wall remember-you, Mr. Speaker, will especially remember-that on the occasion of t'he consideration of the Soldiers' Voting Bill the hon. member for Bonaven-ture and other members on this side of the House very strongly took the ground that any man who enlisted, whether he were under or upwards of 21 years of .age, should be allowed the privilege of voting. The hon. member for Bonaventure contended that if the Canadian boy was fit to be a soldier and to go to the front; if he had sufficient maturity, physical and mental, to engage in the battle for the Empire, he was qualified to exercise .his franchise and to have a voice in deciding how the affairs of Canada as .a part of the Empire should be conducted. The hon. Minister of Justice, who had charge of the Bill, strongly opposed the proposal made by the hon. member for Bonaventure, a proposal which was embodied in the form of an amendment. The Minister of Justice urged very strongly, indeed, that the age limit should be 21. The Solicitor General also urged very strongly that the Bill was right; that there was no reason why Parliament should fix

the age for exercising the franchise at less than 21 years; that the law applying to civilians in the matter of voting should apply also to those who were engaged in the military service. Perhaps I may be pardoned if I refer to the speeches that were made on that occasion. I do so because these gentlemen who to-day are arguing in favour of extending the privilege to our boys under 21 years of age then took a different view; they stood behind the Government in voting upon the amendment moved by the member for Bonaventure. If I am not mistaken, all the gentlemen who have spoken so warmly to-day in favour of this change in the law supported the Government in the view which they took on that occasion. At page 2,344 of Hansard, 1915, I find the following:

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext: Is the minister in a position to tell me what is the youngest age at which these volunteers are accepted? Is there an age limit fixed by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext: I cannot say absolutely that there is an age limit fixed by the department, although I think that ordinary soldiers enlisting are accepted at 18 or 19 years of age, but there are buglers, drummers and boys acting in different capacities.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext: Are there any scouts ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext: There are no boy scouts that I am aware of.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext: I think there are.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
There may be ; I only say that there are none that I am aware of. But there are quite young boys in the position of doing military service, in regard to whom I think the general consensus of opinion would be that they would hardly be of an age at which they could be expected to exercise a mature judgment.
I am not sure whether the Minister of Inland Revenue expressed any opinion on that occasion, but he has recently argued that a man must attain the age of thirty years before he can safely exercise his judgment in such matters. The Minister of Justice proceeded:
Unless for very strong reasons to the contrary, it seemed to those who were responsible for the introduction of the Bill that we must have some degree of maturity, and although it may perhaps be a little beyond what is absolutely required, we thought it the safer course to adhere to the age fixed in the law generally as being the age limit.
Then the member for Bonaventure .said:
Eighteen is the age fixed in the Militia Act for enlistment; I am speaking of the volunteer and not of buglers, drummers or boy scouts. In this case you may have a large number who have enlisted, but who, not having taken the oath as to age, would not become voters. An injustice is being done to the boy of 18, 19 or 20 years, who has enlisted, and who undergoes all the hardships and risks of war, if he is cast aside. I think he will feel that injustice very much, because he knows that he can get the Victoria Cross, the highest distinction for

*valour, no matter what age he is. I am in favour of the principle of giving the soldier a vote if he is a voter. I am also in favour of giving him a vote if he is not a voter, because the service he is rendering to his country entitles him to that consideration,
One would have thought that that argument, made so eloquently by the hon. member tor Bonaventure, would appeal to the hon. gentlemen who have addressed the House in support of this resolution. Mr. Marcil continued:
but I am opposed to the Bill, because I do not think it guarantees that the ballot which the soldier casts will be the ballot which we will receive here. A very great injustice is being done to the boys of over 18 years of age by depriving them of their votes. The minister knows the old verse:
" Mais aux ames bien ndes,
La valeur n'attend pas le nombre des an-ndes."
Boys of 18, 19 and 20, who have the spirit to enlist for the defence of their country, ought to be trusted td cast an intelligent vote. Napoleon Bonaparte was a general in chief of the army at 25. A young man of 18 should be given this right.
The following are the worjls of the Minister of Justice in reply to what many of us would regard as a very convincing argument:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
The boy under 21 years who, being a soldier, is not given the right that is given to a soldier who is over 21, suffers exactly the same injustice as the boy in civilian life of 19 or 20 suffers as compared with the man over 21 who may be in precisely similar circumstances of merit or demerit and who has his vote while the boy under the age of 21 has no vote. It is not only in military careers, but I think we have had cases of early maturity in civil life, one very prominent case being that of a gentleman who became Prime Minister of Great Britain at the age of 21. If the reason of the hon. member is right as regards military circles it ought to be equally right when applied to civilian circles. If it be a good argument that, because we find exceptional cases of maturity developed beyond what one's years would apparently lead one to look for, we should make a general rule departing from the age of 21 years, it would be as applicable to civil life as to military life. I am sorry to hear the expression used that any injustice is intended because after all from the voting point of view all that is to be said is that the boy of 18 does not gain something as compared with the soldier of 21 which he would not have gained had he not been a soldier as compared with any other man in the ordinary walks of life and 21 years of age. Perhaps we have not given, but we have not taken away.
Then Mr. Marcil says:

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
My sole reason for saying
that we should give these boys the right to vote is because they have enlisted. That is the main reason for the wrong, if wrong there be. I do not see why a boy who is capable of bearing arms and serving his country at the age of 18 or 19 years should be debarred from exercising the franchise. The issues of the election may be more fully comprehended by
the young man than the man of maturity. I am sorry that the minister has not extended common justice to those in the ranks above 18 years of age.
My hon. friend the Solicitor General was not convinced by the argument of the hon. member for Bonaventure, because on page 2347 of Hansard he is reported to have said:
What I'arose chiefly to do was to put before the committee my own view as to the question raised by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and repeated by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), as to the extension of the franchise to all soldiers although they have not reached their majority. I take the view that the Bill in that respect is right. I do not look on the extension of the franchise to the soldiers as in any way a quid pro quo, as in any way a benignant action on the part of the state to him in virtue of his soldiership. It appears to me that in regard to the British franchise the law presumes, that if the individual man has a real patriotic interest in his country's affairs, and secondly, if he is competent to express that interest, that man is entitled to vote. We take certain precautions to ascertain whether he lives up to these two requirements-whether he has a real patriotic interest in his country's affairs and whether he is competent to express that interest. We say that he must be a resident, that he must live so long in a certain locality. If he is a rolling stone, we cannot presume that he has that fixed and determined interest that he otherwise will have. On the other hand, in order to ascertain whether he is competent to express his vote or not, we fix the age of twenty-one as the age of maturity at which he arrives at competency. Then we say that a judge by virtue of the restraints of his office is incompetent to express his interest. Then we come here and make an extension of the franchise in one respect; that is, we do not insist upon the condition of fixed residence. To that extent and no more, there is in this Bill an extension of the franchise.
The question came to a vote on April 14, 1915, as hon. gentlemen will see by a reference to Hansard on page 2538. Mr. Marcil then moved, seconded by the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. H. H. McLean) :
That this Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House, with instructions that they have power to amend the same by striking out the words "twenty-one" in the first line of section one and by inserting the word "eighteen" in place thereof.
Mr. Marcil made this further appeal to the House:
The House has already heard the arguments in support of this suggestion. I contend very respectfully that a man who has attained 18 years of age, who has undergone medical inspection, who is mentally and physically qualified to take up arms in the service of his country overseas, and who is willing to make the sacrifice of his life, if necessary, to defend the cause which he has at heart, should be on an equal footing with men of the age of 21. If the soldier who has attained the age of 21

years? is to have the advantage of exercising the franchise, then it is an unjust and unfortunate discrimination that others who are serving their country should be deprived of that right. I think that this view will appeal to the whole of young Canada, which is taking a deep and patriotic interest in this matter.
This amendment was negatived on division. Id I spoke at all upon the subject *on that occasion-and I think I did-I took the view that the franchise sjiould be given to young men of 18 years of age. I know I entertained that view, but I-think all the members on the other side of the House who spoke on this subject expressed views in support of the position taken by the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General, opposing the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Bonaventure. I am glad indeed to see that some hon. gentlemen opposite have changed their minds and that they are now entirely in accord with the views which were then put forward by the hon. member for Bonaventure. It will afford me great pleasure to support the resolution which has been moved by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) who has spoken so eloquently, and I think the speeches which have been delivered so far have presented unanswerable arguments in favour of the resolution.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the difficulty of reaching absolute fairness in the framing of any law is perhaps beyond the capacity of mortal man. In the framing of a franchise law the difficulty of approximating absolute fairness is greater perhaps than in any other sphere of legislation. The resolution introduced by the hon. member for South Perth covers a subject which in its wider scope had been under discussion in Parliament about two years ago. The hon. member's resolution refers only to one branch of the subject that was then before us for legislation, namely, as to whether we would be justified, in view of the very great services rendered their country by those of our military forces who are under the age of 21, in assuming they were both capable of exercising and entitled to the exercise of the franchise. At that time, differences of opinion were expressed in Parliament, and at that time, let me frankly say, I expressed the view that we could not assume both of the qualifications which I thought we should assume before we admitted to the franchise any class of our population.
We undoubtedly could assume that all who had enlisted for service overseas had at 
heart the best interests of their country, and from that standpoint they are undoubtedly entitled to all in the way of franchise that their country can give. I did not feel, however, that we could assume further, that they had by the fact of enlistment reached that age of maturity or that stage of mental development that we could differentiate them from the rest of our population in regard to the franchise. There seems, so far as the debate has gone, to be rather a general impression that we might have well gone farther, or at all events, in view of the far greater sacrifice than was then anticipated by many, we might now reconsider our position and do even more for the soldier than we were prepared to do then. That is undoubtedly the earnest and sincere desire of the mover of the resolution, who has stated his case briefly, concisely and fairly, and the desire in the main of those who have supported him. I do not intimate for one moment that the hon. member for St. John was not sincere in his position that these of our soldiers should be entitled to the franchise. But I do dread what seems to be the manifest truth, that he is not afraid to raise party divisions and antipathies in this House, even though they might result in the wreck of the legislation that he deems so dear. He endeavours to intimate that we on this side of the House took a very, very strong stand and argued most strenuously against this proposal, while on the other side of the House the case was entirely different. Two years ago he tried to make the same question of it, tried with all his might and all his ingenuity; he even went so far as to say that those who took a different position were occupying absurd ground, were arguing absurd contentions in the House. It may surprise hon. members who have not looked up the debates to lear-n that it was not a party question by any means, that there were differences of opinion on both sides of the House, and that on this side of the House the most pronounced, and may I say, the most emphatic, opinion that was expressed in agreement with the present position of the hon. member for South Perth was expressed by the Prime Minister himeelf. It may-surprise even the hon. member for St. John to know that his own distinguished leader who sits to his left (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) spoke words consistent only with the then reading of the Bill, saying on that occasion that the Bill was right and should not be amended. I noticed the hon. leader of the Opposition applauding the hon. member

for fit. John in his reference to myself this afternoon, but I think it would be well for him to read Hansard, 1915, at page 2207, where he gave utterance to the following words when this very point was under discussion :	*
We have laws and regulations the result of the wisdom and experience of ages, which have determined that we may expect the blood and the sacrifice of the soldier and yet that the soldier is not entitled to cast a vote in the administration of the country. That is so in this country; it is so in Great Britain ; it is so in the United States. There are uniform laws governing the exercise of civil and political rights which no nation has yet contravened.
True words, and at no point in his utterances did he even intimate the opinion that it would have been wise for us at that time to contravene those laws and to admit men under 21 years of age to the franchise.

speechtext:
Hear, hear.
#

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
But it is still more interesting in view of what has just been said by the hon. member for St. John, to read the opinion given at that time by another very distinguished member ,of the Opposition, the hon. member for South Renfrew (Hon. Mr. Graham). He did not disguise his view at all. He expressed it very fairly, and certainly just as strongly as did any hon. member on either side of the House. The hon. member for Sputh Renfrew used the following words on page 2350 of Hansard, 1915:
I am strongly of the opinion that 21 is the proper age. I have not heard any good reason...
Although he had heard the hon. member for St. John on several occasions.
I have not heard any good reason advanced why we should change from the age limit that we have always had. After mature deliberation it has been decided in this country that a man has not reached the proper years of maturity at which he is able to vote until he is 21. I do not think the fact of his going to the front changes the principle at all, for a man of 21 years of age is the same at the front as he is at home, loyal and brave and patriotic though he may be.
I d.o not need to go any further, to make it clear to the hon. member for St. John that in: the former debate it would have been scarcely safe for him to characterize those who held views different from his own as absurd, or for him in this debate to endeavour to part the two 'sides of Parliament on such an issue as this; whether we ought to admit men under 18 to the franchise because they are serving their King.
It may be recalled that the Bill introduced in the old House was not a Government. measure. It was introduced by another member and was referred to a committee, which committee, if I recall correctly, dealt with all subjects then befpre Parliament having to do with the franchise, and on the report of the committee the Bill was taken up by the Government and became law.
Mr. PU.GSLEY: Taken up as a Government measure.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext: Became a Government measure, but it was not introduced as such. On the introduction of the Bill, and later during the debate on this point the Prime Minister expressed the view that the other would have been the better course, but undoubtedly he assented constitutionally to the Bill in the form it is in now. Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to put
myself on record as supporting the resolution now before the House and to state the chief motive which actuates me in supporting it, as well as that which caused me to support a somewhat similar resolution brought before the House two years ago by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Hon. Charles Marcil.)

I shall not enter into an argument as to differentiations relating to a division or a vote. When I rise in this House and answer the Speaker "yea" or "nay," I rise with the determination of giving my vote publicly and having it on record. When this matter was before the House two years ago I, for one, advised the Minister of Justice to delay his Bill until the next session. There was no occasion for hurrying at the time; there were two long years within which to frame a Bill which would be more perfect than the one presented by the minister at that time. Had this advice been accepted, the provision which we are now urging, as well as others advantageous tc the soldier, might have been inserted in the Bill.
The chief reason why I support this resolution is that our enlistment has been carried on not by conscription, but by voluntary enlistment. The soldier 18 or 19 yeans of age who is in the trenches to-day went there voluntarily, thus giving indication of his intelligence and of his patriotism. The age of 21 has been recognized all over the world not only as that at which a man may commence to exercise his franchise, but, in every line of business, as the age at which the ordinary human being is capable of assuming the duties of citizenship. A young man has to wait until he is 21 years of age before he is able to administer an inheritance left to him by his father or left to the family of which he is the head. This does not mean that at the age of 18 or 19 a young man is not capable of assuming such duties. It means that Governments have in ordinary cases no evidence upon which they may make a distinction and extend these privileges to any one under the age of 21. But when a young man of 18 is impelled by a sense of duty to fight for his country, thus giving evidence of his intelligence and patriotism, the Government has direct evidence of his capacity to exercise the rights of citizenship as well as the duties pertaining to his family life. It is not only in the universities and colleges that we find young men who are gifted with that degree of intelligence and patriotism. In other walks of life we find them; among the workmen and in our industries, where they rise rapidly by the intelligence with which they have been gifted. Many young farmers at the age of 18 are able to assume the duties formerly carried on by their fathers, and to administer the business of
the farm with as much intelligence and success as if they were 21. The young man, therefore, who gives expression to his intelligence and to his willingness to make the supreme sacrifice for his country, furnishes a criterion upon which a Government may act. To grant these young men the privileges of the franchise would be a recognition of their spirit of sacrifice as well as an encouragement to those who have not yet gone. It is, therefore, with the view of expressing our gratitude to the young men who have gone, as well as to encourage those of 18 and 19 who have not. yet gone, that I ask the Government to forget the past and have a measure passed at once, based on this resolution, which will give the vote to every young man who has gone to fight or who is to go. This is one of the reasons why I support the resolution; concerning many others of less importance, I shall not now take up the time of the House.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is rather refreshing to hear the hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Turgeon) advise the House to forget the past and to deal with questions as they confront us to-day. I do not know that a more stinging rebake was ever addressed to members on his side of the House than that which has been administered by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. In reading the resolution I thought it was one that would appeal to every hon. member of this House.
I think it is advisable that I should read it again, in view of some of the remarks that have fallen from the lips of hon. gentlemen who have already spoken. It is as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should introduce legislation at this session which will extend the franchise to every British citizen who enlisted with the Canadian forces for overseas service, and who was a resident of Canada at the time of enlistment.
This is the question before the House, as introduced by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele), a man who has the reputation of being very fair and very moderate in his views and who does not speak, in the House unless it is on a question that he feels is of vital interest to the country. I believe that his realization of its importance is what caused him to introduce this resolution.
Several other members of the House spoke along similar lines to those followed by the mover of the resolution, but, much to my-

surprise, one of the oldest and most experienced parliamentarians in this House, the hon. member for St. John, had his desk piled up with authorities in an endeavour to fasten something of a recriminatory and political nature that happened two years ago upon hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. When we assembled here on Saturday last and listened with breathless attention to the words of liquid fire that were uttered by the eloquent French statesman who was with us on that occasion, I could not help feeling that during the remainder of thie session there would be less party recrimination, less waste of time, a greater consciousness of the stern duty with which we are confronted, a desire to deal with matters in a fairer manner than we have done in the past. I do not like to recall these things, but just before the House rose at six o'clock, the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) indulged in remarks that were quite uncalled for. He endeavoured to make it appear that we on this side of the House were inconsistent in supporting a resolution of thie kind. I wish to say on my own behalf that when thie question was up on a previous occasion I supported it as strongly as possible. I urged on the Government the advisability of extending the franchise to the men who had been more fully seized of their duty to the State than those who remained at home. There are in the ranks of the Canadian forces to-day grim, silent, battle-scarred veterans of this war who went over with the first contingent and who are not yet 21 years of age. That is something that we did not have two years ago when the matter was before the House; that is something that is well known to every hon. member, and it is a reason why we should carefully consider this resolution which has been introduced by the hon. member for South Perth. Is it right or fair that should an election occur in this country, those men, after two years of hard fighting and undergoing terrible hardships, should be deprived of their right to vote? I am more fully seized of the necessity for a Dominion Franchise Act, universally applicable and uniform throughout the Dominion of Canada, than I have ever been before. If my memory serves me aright, as I have not gone through the records as the hon. member for St. John has done, with a view to finding out certain things that appeal to him, one of the reasons why the' age was fixed at 21 years, was that the age of 21 was fixed in the provin-
cial lisits, which are used in Dominion elections.
There are other matters to be considered in a Franchise Act than merely extending it to our soldiers at the front. We must also put in that Act safeguards that will not render futile the desires and wishes of those men who are fighting on our behalf. Owing to the cosmopolitan character of the population of this country, there are many men in Canada who have not yet become thoroughly Canadianized, men who cherish yet in their breasts a strong sympathy for the countries from which they came, and at the present time we and the Allies are gripped in a death struggle with the countries from' which these men have come. There is this question to be considered in connection with the resolution. Other resolutions affecting the franchise will come up in the course of this session and these matters ought to be taken into consideration together and, as I have stated before, a uniform Act enacted which will meet the requirements of the country. A gradual evolution has been taking place in this country during the past few years. During the last two years we have been confronted with conditions such as have never before been experienced. The wide disparity that exists today in the franchise between the different provinces must be removed in Federal elections ; we must see that safeguards are enacted that will prevent an injustice being done to ourselves, t,o our country, and to the cause for which we are fighting. This resolution is so reasonable and fair that I regret very much that it has not appealed to every hon. member, and that some have, -instead of expressing themselves in favour of it, rather left the impression that they are in favour of it but have stated that somebody on this side of the House or somebody somewhere else had opposed something of a similar nature on a previous occasion. This measure has never been before the H.ouse before, and we are in a better position to-day to realize what is right and fair by those men who are waging this battle on our behalf than we were at any time in the past. I am heartily in favour of the resolution and I believe this resolution and other motions of a similar nature affecting the franchise should be considered and an Act enacted, which will do justice to the occasion and provide safeguards for the interest of our country against the enemy who may be within our gates.
