speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman imply that most of the men who have gone from Canada are Indians?

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
They are not all gone yet anyway. I am sorry that I should be interrupted in this way. In considering questions of this kind, most of us think we ought to pay some attention to what the law of the country is to-day. It is easy enough to introduce resolutions, and I have no doubt in the world that the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) who introduced this resolution this afternoon, did so in good spirit and with a view to conferring the franchise upon the soldiers; but my hon. friend and other hon. members must understand that for the last 20 years or more this House and the Senate of Canada have dealt with this question of the franchise and have practically placed the whole question in the hands of the provinces and have denuded themselves of any power in connection with it. That question has stood the battle and the breeze for over 20 years, and it is not a light matter to come now as we are doing to disturb the whole machinery of government in connection with this matter. Section 10 of chapter 6 of the Revised Statutes of Canada 1906, says:
The qualifications necessary to entitle any person to vote at a Dominion election in any province shall, except as herein otherwise provided, be tho3e established by the laws of that province as necessary to entitle such person to vote in the same part of the province at provincial election.
That is the law of Canada to-day. Each province has the right to say what the franchise shall be, and once that franchise is established by that province it becomes the franchise of the Dominion. I take it that 'the representatives of the different provinces of Canada in the different legislatures are just as loyal as we are and just as appreciative of what belongs of right to the soldiers at the front as we are, and the power is theirs to extend that franchise to the soldiers if they so desire. They have the machinery for the preparation of the lists; there will be no disturbance of the present conditions in any province of Canada if the provincial legislatures so desire to extend the franchise, and I think we should be content with passing resolutions in this House recommending that the different Parliaments in the nine provinces of Canada should do so. If we pass this resolution to-day how are we going to deal with the lists? We have no m-achinery belonging to us in any province in Canada to deal with the lists. For some years we had in this country a Dominion Franchise Act, and I think both Liberals and Conservatives got tired of it. It was repealed by the late Government and a new condition of things brought into play. I was not in Parliament at the time that the Dominion Franchise Act, or the Revising Barristers' Act, as it might be called, was repealed, but I do not think there was any strenuous opposition to its repeal. I have been here for a good many years and I have never heard any Conservative, either a member of Government or a supporter of Government, saying that the old Dominion Franchise Act should come into force; everyone seems to be perfectly content witli the present condition of things. Some of the provincial Governments may be Conservative and others Liberal in their politics, but everyone seems to be content that the preparation of the lists and the conduct of the franchise are carried on fairly and honestly in this country. If the resolution of my hon. friend consisted in a recommendation to the provinces for .an extension of the franchise m any way that would commend itself to my mind I would be more in favour of it, but we aTe taxing ourselves with a great deal of responsibility if we are going to pass a Franchise Act for the soldiers and furnish all the machinery necessary for that purpose. It is not the intention that the votes of soldiers shall be taken at the front, and, therefore, the resolution of my hon. friend is not so important as it appears to be on the surface, because the intention of



the Prime Minister is evidently that the soldiers shall come home before anything is done, and after they return they will be subject to the conditions of the provinces in which Ithey live and the provincial authorities will deal with the subject. At page 41 of Hansard of this year the Prime Minister is reported as having said:-
I know something of the conditions at the front, and I venture to put this thought before the House and the country; the men at the front will be not only practically, but actually, disfranchised if an election does take place in this country while they are in the trenches. That is my conviction. I say they would be actually disfranchised because, although I render every tribute to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the committee which had in hand the preparation of the Soldiers Voting Act of 1915, I am not disposed to think that the arrangements made in that Act or in any other act that could be devised are such as to enable those men to vote, or at least any considerable number of them. You cannot predict what conditions may exist. Supposing an election came on in this country when the fiercest drive of the war was taking place. Do you imagine that the paymasters of those regiments and their commanding officers could busy themselves with handing out ballots to men whose souls were engrossed and whose lives were at stake in the enterprise in which they were engaged? There is something more than that. I say that those men at the front have not it in their heart or their soul to consider matters of party controversy under the conditions with which they are there confronted. I believe those men would want to put aside any one who came to talk to them about political issues or partisan controversy, under conditions of life or of death, of victory or of defeat such as confront them in the trenches or while making a drive to bring this war to an end. Further than that, there may be perhaps a hundred thousand men not in France. You might be able to have some of those men to vote for' Government qr for Opposition, not for a candidate, as provided in the fact alluded to; but do you imagine that those men who are putting their lives to the supreme test in going overseas to fight for their country, will be greatly interested in political issues, or that they will desire to hear political speeches, or that they will welcome the distribution of partisan literature?
This was the Prime Minister's idea of this thing. He thought the men should not be bothered with political matters at all, that they would not stand for speeches or political literature of any kind being distributed among them; they should be left to discharge their duties which they were so worthily discharging. When our soldiers come back from the war, I am sure they will submit themselves to the laws of the different provinces to which they belong, and if this resolution was confined to a recommendation by this House to the different provincial govern-

ments to make what changes in the franchise they deemed advisable on behalf of the soldiers, leaving it to them to decide upon the qualifications as to age and so forth, I would have nothing but commendation for it. But I do not think it is necessary to ask this Parliament to start the huge machinery that would he necessary in order to do something which in the end would amount to nothing, because it is not the intention to take the votes of soldiers while they are away; and when they come back they will of course be satisfied to accept the law as it stansds on the statute -book of the different provinces.

Mr. Speaker, when I hear so much being said and suggested on the other side of the House as to amendments to the. franchise Acts, I fear there is in contemplation some very substantial and radical proposals in respect to the franchise law of the Dominion. As the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has pointed out, as matters now stand, the creation of a federal franchise is entirely governed by provincial statute, and so long as that is the case it seems to me a resolution such as is here proposed is hardly a practical one. However, I did not rise particularly to say that. I yield to no one in my admiration of the gallantry and heroism of thet Canadian soldier. I hope when he returns to Canada there will be a warm spot in every heart and a place at every fireside for him. But I do not see any necessity at this moment for considering seriously the proposal of the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Steele). I think the soldier is more concerned about other matters at the present moment than whether or not a soldier under 21 shall be entitled to vote in the event of a war-time election. The soldier, even though -he be not 21, is a manly man, and I do not think he expects us to reconstruct the established laws of this country to meet his particular case. So far as I know there is no demand from the soldiers concerned for such a change in our law as is proposed in this resolution. After the legislation of 1915 was enacted, I came in contact with a great many soldiers in the city in which I reside, and availed myself of the opportunity to ascertain their opinions on the practicability and advisability of that legislation. I found, of course, differences of opinion, but a great number of them were entirely opposed to the legislation.
I think a more practical question and one far more likely to engage the sympathy

and intelligent consideration of the young soldier at the' front would be, how are we going to provide men in this country to take the place of those who have fallen? Or, what are we going to do to provide for our soldiers who will return to Canada after the cessation of the war? I do not think there is any demand for such legislation as this resolution seeks. I think it would accomplish little good. I have listened very carefully and attentively to the remarks made by hon. gentlemen who have spoken to this resolution, but I have heard nothing which would justify me in expressing my adherence to the principle of the resolution.

Unfortunately, my hon. friend really does not know what he wants, judging from the answer which he was good enough to vouchsafe to my question. The attitude which hon. gentlemen would take towards this resolution would naturally depend somewhat upon what my hon. friend really has in mind. The Solicitor General told us a few moments ago that it was not the intention of the Government to introduce any legislation of ageneral character dealing with the franchise.

My hon. friend proposed the resolution which I read a few moments ago. This resolution purports to ask the Government to introduce legislation this session to extend the franchise to members of the overseas forces under twenty-one years of age. If he wished to effectuate the desire he has expressed in moving this resolution, there is no reason why he should not have introduced a Bill to amend Chapter 11 of the Statutes of 1915 by simply striking out the words "of twenty-one years of age or upwards." He has gone a very long way to work if he really wishes to attain results. Though not a lawyer, he is a professional man and is Chairman of one of the Committees of this House; and I am afraid he is altogether too modest when he puts forward his .supposed lack of legal knowledge as a reason why he did not take the direct course to the object he has in view. His speech to-day showed that he has read the statute. He is aware that it was passed by this House at the instance of the Minister of Justice, and that its introduction was the result not of a mere whim but of a well-considered policy, and that it was fully discussed in the House before its enactment into law. By the method I have suggested he could have proposed the amendment of this statute, and, had he done so, it is probable that by this time his Bill would be before us for second reading and could be crystallized into legislation at once. So I am at a loss to understand what he means by the circuitous method in which he has submitted this matter to the House. If it had been presented in. concrete form as an amendment to the Statute of 1915, so far as I am concerned, the proposition would have bad my zealous and hearty support. There could be no question of it passing, for it was made perfectly clear by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) this afternoon, that my desk-mate, the hon. member for Bonaven-ture (Mr. Marcil) in 1915 moved an amend-mend providing that every one over eighteen years of age should be entitled to a vote if he had enlisted for overseas service. So, had the hon. member for South Perth followed the course that I have suggested hon. gentlemen on this side who voted in 1915 in favour of the resolution of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) would have supported him. Notwithstanding the characteristic argument of the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) it was hon. gentlemen opposite who voted in 1915 that the hon. member for Bonaventure was 
wrong when he proposed to give the franchise to members of the overseas service under twenty-one years of age. No doubt the hon. gentleman (Mr. Steele) forgot that the issue had been raised. Of course, the Solicitor General must needs attempt to show that my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), in calling attention to the fact that my desk-mate had proposed this change two years ago, was playing politics. Of course he does not mean these little pleasantries-

speechtext:
-which hon. members on the other side have now discovered, apparently for the first time, ought to be done. At that time they did not want it done. Let me remind the Solicitor General, with regard to the homilies he is fond of delivering concerning hon. members on this side, of the old proverb, evil is to him who evil thinks. He must not believe that because he happens to sit on the treasury benches that he alone is the embodiment of statesmanship, and that he could not possibly descend from his high pedestal and himself engage in talking politics. He knows that he makes that descent often; that he has to; that when hon. gentlemen opposite get into trouble he is the Moses who is called upon to lead them out of that trouble. Of course, he thoroughly believes that on such occasions he is not playing politics, but is performing a high and patriotic duty. And equally, of course,

when my hon. friend from St. John, in that kindly manner of his, suggests in all candor that we on this side were prepared to put this amendment on the statute books which the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) wants us to support to-day, the Solicitor General deems it his patriotic duty to rise in his might and denounce my mild and kindly friend on the ground that he is endeavouring to introduce politics. I think the Solicitor General had better refrain from these homilies, for wisdom will not die with hon. gentlemen opposite, nor *patriotism either.
I regret that this proposal has not been brought before the House in the form of an amendment to this Act. Let me point out that my hon. friend from Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) is right in his criticism. The unquestioned policy of this country for many years has been to accept the franchise as laid down by the provincial legislatures, having in view the fact that they are in touch with local conditions and have control in matters of municipal organization. Many years ago there was a question between the parties as to a federal franchise, but that has long since disappeared. We now follow the system which obtains in every great federation of states, the franchise of the several states being accepted. As has been suggested, that is our position with regard to woman suffrage. Certain provinces have decided that their women shall have the right to vote, while certain other provinces have not so far accepted the principle of women suffrage. The right to vote given to females in certain provinces is recognized under our statute so far as those provinces are concerned. The only exception to our legislation upon that subject was made in the Bill introduced by the Minister of Justice in 1915, and now appearing in our statute book as chapter 11 of the statutes of that year. We were then creating machinery under which the votes of the men who were overseas, or congregated in camps in Canada, Bermuda or elsewhere, might be recorded. We were not so much making a new franchise law but rather a new electoral law. But incidentally to the providing of machinery for the taking of this vote, there was introduced a clause to give the franchise to every man pf the overseas forces, twenty-one years or over, who was a British subject, no matter what his residence or his property qualification. This, I say, is the only exception that has been recognized in this Parliament for a long time to the principle that the provinces
shall fix the franchise. I am glad to know from the Solicitor General that it is not the desire to depart from this accepted principle.
I am inclined to support the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Steele) on the assumption that it is his desire to ask the Government to introduce an amendment to the Act of 1915, so as to provide that every member of the overseas forces who is a British subject shall be entitled to vote. It seems to me this is a proposition concerning which there cannot be much question. As to the position, in this relation, of the Indians, that is a very large question, and one involving grave considerations. There may be provinces in which, though the Indians are wards of the Government and dependent upon the bounty of the citizens of Canada for their support, the argument might be in favour of extending to them the right to vote. But in other provinces there are conditions which make it impossible to give to these people, who are the children of the state, the right to exercise the franchise jointly with the citizens. I do not wish, therefore, to be understood as acceding to the proposition that this amendment, providing that those who are under 21 years of age shall have the right to vote, can be made so general as to give recognition to the proposition that Indians shall be given the Tight to vote. The conditions are entirely different. It is questionable whether there is any necessity for this legislation at all. In some of the provinces-I know of two already-legislation has been passed which provides that every person who has gone overseas shall have the right to vote. Two of the western provinces have, by amendment to their Franchise Acts, provided that that shall be done, and in at least one of the Maritime Provinces a similar provision has been made.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to draw the attention of the House for a moment to the question that arises in the minds of several hon.

gentlemen as to whether it is the intention of my toon, friend from South Perth (Mr. Steele) merely to amend the Act to give votes to soldiers while reducing the age at which they are entitled to exercise the franchise from 21 to 18 years, or whether it is the intention to change the electoral machinery entirely and take the privilege of providing the voters' lists away from the different provinces. In several of the provinces they have already taken action with regard to the exercise of the franchise .by soldiers. Last year the legislature of New Brunswick made .an amendment to the Elections Act providing that all soldiers, whether overseas or at home, and whether their names were enrolled on the voters' lists or not, should be entitled to vote at elections. The section reads as follows:-
Who at any election held during the present war, or within the calender year next succeeding the declaration of peace, if he shall have served in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, or in the British Army or on Home Service in the present war, was at the time of his enlistment a feona fide resident of, and domiciled in the province of New Brunswick, and is at the time of tendering his vote a bona fide resident of, or domiciled in the district in which such vote is tendered; provided that no person discharged from service because of misconduct shall be qualified to vote under this sub-section.
So, the province of New Brunswick provided that all soldiers should be entitled to vote whether they had served overseas or in home defence? During the election held in New Brunswick in February a number of soldiers came to the polls and cast their ballots. Their names were not on the lists but they came there according to this Act and exercised their franchise. There was some question whether, under the Act, a .soldier under the age of 21 years could vote, but both parties, anxious that the soldiers should exercise the franchise, offered no objection and any soldier who appeared at the poll was allowed to cast Ms ballot. I understand from my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Boss) that they have made provision for the soldiers' votes in Ontario-, they have done so in the western provinces, I do not know about Nova Scotia, hut I have no doubt that the different provinces will enact legislation with regard to the soldiers' vote. It seems to me it is interfering with provincial rights when we attempt to legislate with regard to the franchise and that the question had better be left to the respective provinces. In. so far as I have been able to learn, the experiment is. my own province has worked out most satisfactorily.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not purpose making .any extended observations on this resolution, but I desire to say that I shall support it. There i.s -a certain amount of principle involved in the resolution and I think we should steadily keep in mind the principles that should govern with respect to the granting of the franchise either for federal and national purposes or provincial and local purposes. If history has taught us anything it has taught us at least 'that the exercise of the franchise is a matter of very serious import to the life of the state. It has taught us that we have men within the state who have now the right -to exercise the franchise who, at least, are not the supporters of the state and its great enterprises to the extent to which they should be. Now, I lay down two- principles that must govern in -a matter of this kind. First, in respect to local and provincial matters, the provinces .should be the best and, in fact, the only, judges as to who should vote. Men and women can vote and vote freely upon local issues, on matters that are not beyond the competence of a provincial legislature but when it comes to matters affecting the national well-being, the life of the state, the very existence and destiny of this Dominion. I submit that only those persons who are nationals, using the word " nationals " in the sense in which it is used in the hooks, should be permitted to exercise the franchise. In matters of life .and death to the state, in matters of. the existence of our identity .as a nation, only tho.se persons who are nationals should be permitted to vote. Who are nationals? The first among all nationals .are those men who have offered their lives in defence, of our common country and our civilization. I do not care whether they are 21 years of age or not; they .have offered their lives upon the battlefields of Europe in defence of our civilization, of our institutions .and of our lives and surely they should not be denied the vote. On what principle should they be denied the vote? Could any man give any greater evidence of love of country or devotion to its. institutions than to offer his life as every man did who joined the expeditionary forces? I repudiate in toto the doctrine of the hon. member for Pic-tou (Mr. Macdonald) who said that an Indian shall not vote who- offers himself for service overseas. Whether it be right o.r wrong I state it .as my own personal view that any member of an aboriginal tribe who leaves Canada and offers his life in defence

of our liberty should not be denied the right to say -something as to what shall be the destiny and the future of this great Dominion. I merely s-ay that is my personal view as it strikes me at the present moment.
The first of those who must be acknowledged as Nationals are the men who offer' their lives, -by reason of having volunteered for overseas service; the second classification of those who are Nationals and entitled to vote on Federal or National affairs, are those who are British subjects; the third would be those who. are naturalized, plus probably something more, because the exercise of the Federal franchise, the exercise of the power to determine the national destiny of Canada, involves, as we have learned by studying the history of this country during the last three years and the history of our friends to the south and of our people overseas, something more than -mere naturalization-it involves some assimilation to the institutions of our country, some knowledge of the history of our traditions, some love and reverence for the great names that have given us our civilization, liberty and freedom-and that can come, I submit, only from something more than mere naturalization, something more than merely living three years in the state and swearing before a Justice of the Peace something which a man does not understand, and does not care whether he understands or not. We at least should learn something from this waT, and if we have learned anything I repeat, Sir, it must be that the life of the state can be entrusted only to those who are Nationals -in the sense in which that word is used. Therefore I classify them once more as (1^ those who have gone overseas, offered themselves for service overseas, offered their lives, if need be, in defence of the state; (2) those who are British subjects; (3) those who are naturalized within the state and have had a training that has enabled them to have assimilated something of our institutions and some love for our traditions and history.
And then a further question arises, whether or not you shall place a limitation upon thaf right; and it seems to me that no thoughtful man who has -read the history of this -country will fOT a single moment deny that you should refuse the Federal franchise to those who owe allegiance to a foreign state of a military character. In other words, the reservists of a foreign state should never be permitted to exercise the Federal or National franchise.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext: You include the Allies?

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
The Allies have
nothing to do with the principle, nothing at all. The men who are interested in the preservation of Britain are British subjects by birth or naturalization, and those who have given the further indications that I have mentioned. It well may be-I pray it may not be - that in this country we may again see, as I saw some years ago, men rush to the colours of a foreign country, not our ally. I saw men from Canada rush to the colours of Serbia 9 p.m. when she was not an ally o-f Great Britain. They had become naturalized in this country, but when the call came from overseas, they rushed to the defence of their civilization on the plains of Serbia and in the Balkans. That is unsound, so far as the exercise of a national franchise is coneerned. No man who owes allegiance to a foreign power of a military character, no man who can be- summoned at the call o-f a foreign power, whether allied to this country or not, should be permitted to exercise a voice in determining the national destiny of this Dominion.	.
I submit those principles as being principles that should govern with respect to the exercise of the franchise in this country, and if these be sound principles-and I submit that this is a sound statement df the case-then all men, whether they be eighteen or nineteen or twenty or twenty-one years of age, it matters not, who have fulfilled the first requisite of indicating -by their conduct and their action, 'by their splendid patriotism, and willingness if need be to sacrifice life itself in defence of the liberties of this country and of our -common civilization, should be granted the franchise.
I therefore do most heartily support this resolution, remembering further that -this matter engaged two years ago the attention of a parliamentary

committee of which. I happened to be a member. The consensus of opinion in this House then was that the limit should still Ibe maintained at twenty-one years of age. I was not one of those who then so thought; nor have I changed my opinion. I can only reiterate the statements I have made, that any man, whatever be his age, if he be physically fit and old enough to be accepted for service overseas, if he has shown that he has such a stake in our destiny, such an interest in our future, such a great and abiding faith in our civilization and

destiny, that, if need be, he is willing to offer life itself in defence of our liberties, should be granted the fullest rights of citizenship. If, while we gather in this Chamber and discuss paltry resolutions and display bitterness and strife, this man is willing to make the supreme sacrifice, are we to deny him the greatest of all privileges that a free man can exercise, that of expressing his will with respect to the destiny of the State?
There are other matters that might be discussed upon this resolution. I was not present this afternoon and do not know what has been said. I have heard only the observations of the hon. gentleman from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), of the hon. gentleman from Westmorland (Mr. Copp), and a few words from my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. iSteele); but I desire to place myself on record as being heartily in support of a resolution which will grant to my fellow Canadians overseas who have offered their lives in defence of the liberties we enjoy in this Chamber, the right, by their voice and vote, to determine what shall be the future of this great Dominion. We should be less than men if we should endeavour to deny that right to any man, black or white, red or yellow, who is a citizen of this country by birth or naturalization, who has shown his patriotism to be of such a type that he is willing to sacrifice his life for our country. That is the view I take of the principles that must guide us in deciding who should exercise the franchise within this country upon great national questions involving the life, the integrity, the destiny of Canada-and more, of that Empire of which Canada is to-day the most prominent dominion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) with a great deal of interest, as we always do. So far as the first proposition which he puts forward is concerned, I do not think there has been very much division among the members of this House who have spoken since the debate commenced this afternoon. Of course, there is always this question, whether a man under twenty-one years of age has given matters of state sufficient attention to be enabled to cast an intelligent vote. There is a great deal in what the hon. member for Calgary said, that a man who risks his life should have a right to say what the policy of this country shall be. I do not quarrel with my hon. friend in that, but, in my judgment, the

hon. member for Calgary has opened up another phase of discussion which I should like to see elucidated, to have a little more light thrown on it, because there is something behind his remarks that has hardly been made plain. He lays down the principle that a man who is a British subject -by birth or naturalization shall have the right to vote, but he seems to have an idea that there is some other class of men who are really British subjects who- should not have the right to vote. I should like to know to what class he refers. He has spoken of the Serbian reservist who is a British subject as one of this class. That is not the fault of the Serbian reservist, but of the naturalization law. This country has invited into it people from all parts of the earth, and we have had a law that a man who has resided in Canada for three years with the intention of settling in it and has complied with certain conditions, taken the oath of allegiance and fulfilled conditions of residence, is entitled to naturalization, and once he is so entitled, so long as he is in Canada he is entitled to all the rights of a British subject. How is my hon. friend going to take from that man his right to -the franchise?

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext: The Privy Council so decided in the Japanese case. The Privy Council has decided that it was competent for the Legislature of British Columbia to say that a Japanese should not exercise the franchise, although he was a British subject.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
I suppose that Parliament is all-powerful in anything over which it .has jurisdiction. Under the present law, the legislature of a province is all-powerful in the matter of who shall have the rights of the franchise. But take the case of a man who has complied with all requirements, has lived in Canada for three years, has taken the oath of allegiance and has become a naturalized British subject. It is monstrous that some person like the hon. member for Calgary should say: it is true that we invited you into this country under certain promises and conditions, but, for some reason, I do not want you to vote; therefore I am not going to give you the right to do so. I am glad that the hon. gentleman has made himself a little plainer.
I think I am in the judgment of the House when I say that he stands practically alone in the position which he takes; anyway, I hope that he does. If there is fault anywhere, it is in the naturalization law. The naturalization law was amended a couple

of years ago, making it a little harder for a man to be naturalized-and I would not mind if it went further still. But I do hope that my hon. friend is not forecasting a, change of policy on the part of this Government, this Parliament or this country.
I know of no greater misfortune that could happen to Canada than that she should violate pledges made to the people of Europe in by-gone years when she invited them here.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext: The Privy Council has said that there was no such promise and no such pledge. The franchise is neither a promise nor a pledge. It is a privilege which the legislature-

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENFRANCHISE EVERY MAN ENLISTED IN CANADA.
speechtext:
Notwithstanding my hon. friend's learned remarks, I do not care a straw for what the Privy Council said. The people of Canada know the conditions under which these people have been invited here, and they will know if the rights which were promised to them are withheld. But, Sir, we are travelling far afield. I thought that it was not right to allow such a revolutionary statement to go by unchallenged, and I hope that if my hon. friend or his friends have any such ideas in their minds, they will state them openly and not in veiled manner, as did the hon. member for Calgary.
Subject to what has been said in this respect, I do not think that there is much difference of opinion as between the two sides of the House or among individual members as to the motion that is now under discussion. As has been pointed out, provision has been made in a number of the provinces by which soldiers may vote, regardless of their age. With that provision I have no objection. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Westmorland, it worked all right in the New Brunswick elections in February last, and I assume that it will work all right wherever it is tried. But, as was remarked by the member for Pictou, I do submit that if the House is going to take any action in the matter, it ought to be done simply by an amendment to the Act of 1915.
On the motion Of Mr. A. A. McLean (Queens, P.E.I.), the debate was adjourned.

subtopic: PROPOSED UTILIZATION OF CANADIAN FUEL RESOURCES.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is of great importance that the increased and increasing demand for fuel for manufacturing and residential purposes be supplied in larger quantities and at cheaper rates than are now possible; that the deposits of bituminous and anthracite coal in Canada, located in the extreme eastern and western portions thereof, be more fully and thoroughly utilized for the benefit of the residents of the central provinces ; that the enormous peat and lignite deposits so widely distributed through all portions of the Dominion be also scientifically made use of for the same purpose and further that the Government of Canada make a special effort, through legislation and otherwise, to have these valuable deposits more fully and rapidly developed to the end that the people of Canada may be adequately supplied with these fuels.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution which I present to the House is one which is worthy of the closest attention of every member. We have in Canada the most wonderful undeveloped mineral resources of any country in the world. We have connected with the Mines Department at Ottawa an excellent staff which is capable of undertaking any work that may be assigned to them, and, while I find that there is some overlapping in the work done, much good is accomplished. I am glad that the Minister of Mines has furnished rooms where the specimens of our mines, gathered over the last seventy years, can be exhibited. The samples of materials and of products from different parts of our country which are on exhibition deserve our attention. These specimens were, until a few weeks ago behind closed doors, locked in vaults, boarded up in cellars and in places where it was impossible to have them properly displayed-through no fault of the Minister of Mines.
It is my belief that, at the close of this war no branch of industry in Canada outside of agriculture will receive as great a stimulus as will the mining industry, and I respectfully urge upon the Government the need of devoting its best energies to render every assistance it can to the development of the industries which are connected with the Mines Department. Important matters of research and constructive work connected with the Mines Department must not be left in abeyance.
Since this war began, every nation has been compelled to re-examine and investigate her material resources. Canada possesses tremendous resources in forests, * fields, and mines. Let us commence at once to investigate and utilize them.
While investigating this subject, I have been greatly impressed by the number of products manufactured in the United States and England out of the raw material that has been taken from Canadian mines

Education, organization, and scientific research are needed in connection with this department, and a general speeding up pf the whole organization is desirable. When the war is over, we should have, and I believe will have, a properly co-ordinated mineral survey of the Empire, and Canada should lead the way. Canada should have some means of demonstrating just what Canadian mines can and dp produce. Research and constructive work must be carried on with greater energy tl^an ever before. Educational work regarding our mineral resources should not be confined to our high schopls and collegiate institutes, as it is to a large extent to-day, but public schools should make the subject attractive.
The chief statistician of the Department of Mines, Mr. John McLeish, reports that the value of the mineral output of Canada last year was $33,000,000 greater than in 1915. The advance was not mainly due tp the rise in prices, for the tonnage also increased remarkably. In 1886 the value was $10,221,255; in 1896 it was $22,474,256; in 1906, $79,286,697, and ten years later, $170,000,000.
At the present rate of development we may expect that during the year 1917 the output of the mines of Canada will exceed $200,000,000. The stimulus given to Canadian mineral development by the war is great and probably permanent. One of the problems which confront Canada to-day, is to devise the best means of rendering available the various supplies of low grade fuel.
Last winter every great city in Canada was within 48 hours of starvation owing tc lack of fuel. In recent years we have had two coal famines, first in 1901-2, the year of the coal miners' strike, and secondly, this year, when the severity of the weather and the extraordinary prosperity in the United States caused an unprecedented congestion of freight. A survey of conditions in the United States demonstrates that in the future there will be more coal famines than in the past, and that they will occur at shorter intervals. The current issue of Coal Age, in New York, says that the reserves of coal usually held over by the big companies are completely exhausted.
Dr. George Otis Smith, Director of the United States Geological survey, commenting upon the world's supply of coal, and with particular reference to the reserves in his own country, states:
This glance at the world's reserves of coal shows plainly not only that the United States leads all other countries in production, our 
annual output being nearly 40 per cent of the total, but also that it possesses the greatest reserves. Yet in respect to no mineral is there greater need to emphasize the folly of export-, ing the raw material. Let us keep our coal at home, and with it manufacture whatever the world needs.
The people of Canada just now are gaining an impression, at considerable inconvenience, of what it would mean were the United States for any reason to cut off Canada's coal supply. Presumably there are insufficient facilities and motive power for coal transport. Cities and towns in Canada are keeping fires alight with practically a day-to-day supply of coal, and the time may come when the United States may deem it expedient to reserve her supply of coal for her own use.
Many reasons are given for the making of the coal congestion, namely, zero weather, heavy snow falls, difficulty of obtaining men on the railroads and in the shops, shortage of motor cars and enlistment of men. Railroad officials appear to be doing their best to meet the difficulties. The industries of Toronto, Hamilton, and western Ontario, seem to be the greatest sufferers and universities and schools have closed owing to the shortage of coal. The situation is most serious and an adequate remedy must be found.
I have taken a number of clippings from newspapers which have appeared within the last few weeks, and the headings on some of these articles are:
Coal famine may tie up industry.
Investigate coal shortage in States.
Coal embargos to be modified.
What wage Increase to miners means to consumers.
New York, April 26.-Coal men estimate. that the wage increase granted to 175,000 miners in the anthracite fields will raise the retail price of hard coal an average of sixty cents a ton. The agreement signed last night by representatives of the operators and the United Mine Workers of America adds approximately $3 0,000,000 a year to the miner's wages and is the largest increase awarded in the history of anthracite industry.
Coal fails; schools close.
Canadian roads hard hit by the price of coal; The coal bill of the Canadian Railways will show an increase of more than $8,000,000 this year.
United States petroleum resources are becoming exhausted. A thirty-six per cent falling off in the production.
Lay in your supply of coal is the advice: L. E. Tillson says it may go up to from $10 to $15 a ton.
Must increase Nova Scotia coal mine output.
Coal men now have additional worries: possibilities of miners' strike and advanced freight rates threaten situation here.
Civic trading in food and fuel: legislation gives municipalities chance to curb cost of living : may build storehouses.

About three years ago the head of the Geological Survey Department of the United States sent a strong recommendation to Congress urging that the export of anthracite coal out of the United States should be stopped, giving as a reason that about two-thirds of the deposits of anthracite coal in the United States had already been exhausted and that the people of the United States were facing a condition which if carried on at the present rate of consumption of this coal would deplete the mines available for this supply of coaJ, within the next hundred years. This statement has been discussed with a great deal of emphasis in different parts of the United States. It has been favourably commented upon by many prominent men, and the condition is such as to warrant our immediate attention.
If the United States were -to place an export duty on their coal to Canada, we would be then compelled to do what we ought to do to-day, to look about for a source of supply of fuel to take care of our great requirements in this regard. We would ' then begin to realize that some effort should be made for the development of the poorer grades of fuel that are available almost at our very door.
The attention of geologists and mine owners, also the general public, especially during the past year, have been directed to the questions of the coal supplies and reserves in Canada, and on the Continent. The large increase in the consumption of coal in recent years makes this question of vital importance to this country. Only last year, for instance, we imported $42,000,000 worth of coal into Canada. Considering the constant increase in our imports I think hon. gentlemen will agree that this matter should receive out closest attention.
Canada has large supplies of coal situated in the Atlantic and Paoific regions; in the mountains of British Columbia and in the Plains regions of the Central Interior. On the Atlantic and Pacific seaboards, bituminous coals are extensively mined. The interior fields supply coals of various kinds, the coals of the mountains being the most important and of the highest grade. The province of Alberta forms Canada's largest coal reserve. The coal areas of Canada have an estimated total surface extent of one hundred and nine thousand one hundred and sixty-eight square miles.
In summing up the reports of the coal deposits in the world, Canada stands second among the nations in regard to her deposits.
Canada has 1,234,269 millions of tons available; the United States has 3,838,659 million tons available. Great Britain has only 189,000 millions of tons; Germany has
423,000	millions of tons .available. At Pic-tou, N.S., coal fields show an actual available supply of 390 million tons. In addition to this, the small fields and the estimated coal area in Nova Scotia will .amount to 400 millions of tons. The present output of coal fox Nova Scotia is about 3,000,000 of tons per annum. The coal is largely consumed in the East, much is exported, and a large quantity comes to Montreal.
We have only two ..deposits of anthracite coal worthy of mention in Canada. One is located in the Bocky Mountains, and the other in the Yukon. Neither of these is easy of access, nor capable of very great development. We use anthracite in our homes because of less smoke and smell. In the West they manage to keep fires in the houses all night with low grades of coal. If our furnaces w-ere changed to consume the smoke, we could use the lower grades of coal with comfort. Mr. Dowling, Canada's coal expert, says this can he done,, and we can use $5 coal instead of $8 or $10 coal and get more heat units per ton out of it by adapting our furnaces and heating appliances to its use. From Brandon,'Manitoba, east to the Atlantic coast, we are almost entirely dependent upon the United States for our anthracite coal for cooking and heating purposes.
The anthracite coal deposits of North America are fast becoming exhausted. The Americans admit that they have used twro-thirds of their total supply, and so we must expect that anthracite will increase in value as the years go by. We must therefore, investigate more closely our soft coal deposits and make every effort to develop them economically. We must also induce our people to make use of the tar-products taken from soft coal which are most valuable. One of the principal products taken from soft coal is ammonium sulphate, which iis used extensively as a fertilizer. We are now making a lot of toluol from Canadian soft coal taken out at Sydney Mines. This same firm has been making coke for the steel plants for years past. Soft coal can be transported from two ports in Nova Scotia, namely, Sydney and Piotou. This coal could go through our canals up the lakes to Port Arthur, and -might be able to compete in price with the soft coal brought from the United States, which is delivered to the ports along our inland .-waters. This

subject requires immediate investigation. Should an embargo be placed on coal coming into Canada from the United States this seems the most feasible way of" supplying the cities on our inland waters. The Government should inquire into the feasibility of handling grain east and coal west.
To obtain coal of a similar grade to that mined in Nova Scotia we have to go to the Rocky Mountains eight hundred miles west, of lyinnipeg. [DOT] For lower grades of soft coal, nearly the whole of the province of Alberta and the southern part of the province of Saskatchewan can be called one immense coal field. Some districts in southern Saskatchewan contain soft coal from ten to thirty feet in thickness, but it is of such a nature that when it is exposed to the air it dries to a powder.
Some definite effort should be made to develop the immense soft coal area in southern Saskatchewan. The Department of Mines know where the seams and exposures are located in the bulk of this immense coal field. Experiments have been made in Ottawa by the Mines Branch within the past few years which have gone to show that lignite coal similar to that located in Saskatchewan, when used in a gas producer, can be as economically handled as regards power as if it were anthracite, provided it is used in the localities where the coal is produced. The day may come when the power used in the great cities of our West will be produced at the mines. How can we make that coal in a shape that it can be shipped to other parts of the Dominion? We have demonstrated that it can be economically produced and used in the area where the mines are located, but what can be done to prepare it for export to other districts? Across the line from Saskatchewan, in Dakota, they have the same product. The University of Dakota took up the question of coal development. They tried to dry the coal and briquette the dust. Their early experiments were not successful, when exposed to the moisture in the air these briquettes would go to pieces. The next examination was to test the t^oseibility of treating the coal to make charcoal and then briquetting it. The result of this experiment is satisfactory and some effort should be made to develop this idea in Canada. Mr. Dowling is satisfied that a proper handling of soft coal in Saskatchewan could be made with briquetting it, and that this fuel would soon take the place of anthracite for home consumption, and would also

take the place of fuel for power purposes on the railways and in the manufacturing plants that are not already provided with gas.
As to the question of substitutes: For years in Germany there has been an absolute embargo on the soft coals and the lignites. They compel these all to be roasted and the tars and ammonium compounds extracted, before the charcoal or coke can be burned. The residue is a heavy coke, which takes the place of anthracite. This is one way of using the poorer grades of coal to advantage. The limit for hauling soft coal advantageously by the railway in the West at present is about Brandon, Manitoba. Ohio soft coal comes by water, and is handled at Port Arthur, the railway haul towards the west is cheaper than the railway haul towards the east, with grain and products being shipped from the West, the briquettes could be handled with advantage as far east as Winnipeg or Port Arthur.
Between Winnipeg and Montreal there are, generally speaking, no coal deposits. Therefore, the supply to the people and industries, between Winnipeg and Montreal must* come from the United States or be shipped in from Nova Scotia by boat up the lakes. Nova Scotia coal is a good grade of soft coal, and by the treatment just referred to, namely, the coking treatment, would form a good substitute for anthracite.
We 'have only one small area of lignite coal in Ontario and Quebec, and that is of a very inferior quality. It is located on the Moose River, James Bay slope, not far from the Transcontinental. It is in clay about twenty feet below the surface. The seams are only about three or four feet in thickness and would be most expensive and difficult to operate.
Electricity has given tremendous assistance in conserving our coal. It is said that if the electric power already established in Canada were dispensed with it would be necessary to import twice as much coal as is at present consumed in order to supply our people. By developing electricity we have made enormous savings in fuel, and we should investigate at once and see how much farther we can go in this regard. If we nationalize our railroads the Government may feel justified in electrifying large portions of our main lines, and in this way conserve the coal for other purposes. The Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway hauls by electric power freight and passengers over 440 miles of its road, and is at present electrifying an additional 250 miles.

The officers of the road claim to have solved the coal supply problem, and the cost of operation by electricity is on'ly one-third that of operation by steam. In addition to this, one-third of all the equipment formerly used for the transportation of fuel has been released, and they claim to have doubled the capacity of the single line. Snow troubles, they also say, axe nearly eliminated and extreme cold has little effect on operation. Canada, with her immense water powers in the East and Central Provinces, and abundance of cheap coal in ithe West, may soon electrify the main lines, thereby conserving her fuel,
and use her steam equipment for branch and short hauls.
The British Empire is now known to possess very large reserves of coal. It is estimated that its share is very nearly one-quarter of the world's reserve. As one-half of the world's supply is estimated to be in territory owned by the United States of America, the present known supply for all the remaining nations is about equal to that of the British Empire.

Canada appears to be an important storehouse, but, although it has large reserves, much of this is not available for the commerce of the Empire. Important supplies are, however, to be found on both the Atlantic and Pacific seaboards and may compete with foreign fuels.
The cretaceous rocks exposed in the western part of Manitoba are all marine deposits. Thin streaks of coal occur in this sandstone formation. Light-coloured shades appear in Turtle Mountain near the interior boundary line. In the lower slopes small lignite seams have been discovered. Professor Dowling claims that an estimate of the amount of coal covers a very small area of the ^slopes on the west of these hills, where the lower seams are workable.

The ordinary growth of our provinces calls for cheaper power and cheaper fuel; and the development of our western provinces will depend to a large extent on the supply of cheap fuel and power. For, notwithstanding the existence of the enormous deposits of cbal in the extreme eastern and western portions of Canada, certain of the provinces are dependent on foreign sources for their supply. Conditions, however, may not continue as they are to-day. They may change suddenly and we may find ourselves deprived of fuel from the United States without warning. For such an event, we have made no provision; we have accumulated no extra store to meet such an emergency, but import only what is needed annually. For some time past, the strikes in the coal mines of the United States have demonstrated that conditions such as I have

mentioned must be reckoned with, while other causes than strikes, such as the great development of industries, and the demands of the railways for supply during the war, may deprive us for long periods of' this outside source of fuel. It is, therefore, wise for us to make provision for an emergency and seek within our own territory the means of supplying this all important necessity. Fortunately, nature has provided a substitute for coal and wood in the peat bogs scattered throughout our central provinces.
The population of our towns and cities is composed largely of wage earners. Our climate, for at least four or five months of the year, requires a large amount of fuel for family use; cheap and abundant fuel is a necessity of existence. There are cities in Canada where families are herded together with insufficient space for health and civilized life, because of the cost of fuel in the winter.
It may be safely said that there will be no permanent reduction in the price of coal; rather it is reasonably certain that there will be a gradual hut steady increase. Fuel will become higher as the years go by. The cost of development of heat from water power, in addition to maintenance and management, does not encourage us to believe that we will be able to use electricity as a poor man's fuel for many, many years to come. The price of anthracite and other coals is advancing largely because of exhaustion of the thicker beds, and increased costs of working, freight and transportation facilities. Anthracite coal is fast becoming the fuel of the rich.
In addition to this, manufacturing establishments are bound to increase and the coal consumption for power purposes will likely develop more rapidly. As coal becomes dearer, the difficulty and uncertainty of the supply becomes more accentuated, and the importance of a substitute fuel becomes more rfrgent. If, therefore, the great peat bogs of Canada could be successfully converted into fuel which would be cheaper than wood or coal the advantages thus conferred upon the future inhabitants of Canada and the United States could hardly be overestimated. The difficulties to be overcome do not appear to me to be very gieat when the attendant benefits are taken into consideration. The kinds of fuel available in Canada are:
The wood still standing.
Our oil deposits.
The oil contained in oil shales.

Gas.
Lignite coal.
Water powers (or white coal).
Anthracite coal.
Bituminous coal.
And our peat deposits.
Peat is incipient coal. It is made up of the more or less thoroughly decomposed and carbonized remains of plants accumulated under conditions that have prevented their complete transformation into gaseous and mineral matter. The successive stages in the process of carbonization, as it is reported in nature, is first peat, then lignite coal, anthracite and graphite, a form of carbon. For centuries, peat has been extensively used for domestic fuel by the peasantry of northern Europe. An important source of additional fuel for the more immediate future in Canada exists in our extensive peat bogs. These, and the great lignite areas of the northwest occupy a middle ground between coal on the one hand and such vegetable fuels as wood, etc., on the other.
With the reductica in our forest area, due to settlement and other causes, and the consequent rise in fuel prices, the development of these latent resources has become a matter of general and immediate concern. The development of these resources should proceed along such lines, and by such methods, as will secure the maximum of economic return.
For many years past efforts have been made to develop the peat areas in Ontario and Quebec. A large amount of money was frittered away by careless and useless endeavours to produce this material in a manner in which it might be marketable. However, some six years ago the Government decided to make a practical investigation into the peat producing areas of our country, and, if possible, demonstrate the advantages to be derived from peat production. They sent representatives to Holland, Sweden, Denmark, Germany and Russia to gather data and material that could be utilized to advantage in Canada. On the return of these representatives the Government purchased 300 acres of the peat bog at Alfred, about forty, miles out of Ottawa, and prepared to demonstrate the commercial feasibility of the manufacturing of peat fuel by the employment of a process which is well known in Europe, and which was the only process for manufacturing peat economically. The Government manufactured 2,000 tons of peat in that bog; they sold this peat in Ottawa and vicinity to

householders and manufacturers for the purpose of introducing that form of fuel to the public and to obtain expressions of opinion regarding this fuel for domestic purposes. The various users of this fuel almost invariably expressed their satisfaction with peat as fuel. They further expressed their keen desire to continue the use of this fuel. I have 150 letters from people who used peat as fuel, and, with the exception of two or three, all speak in the highest terms of its heating qualities, its economy and efficiency.
After the completion of their experimental work, the Mines Branch felt that they had accomplished all that they should do, i.e., the demonstration that this peat could be manufactured at a low cost and transported economically, and that as a fuel it was satisfactory. The Mines Branch felt that further development should be left to private indiyiduals. They disposed of the plant and acreage to a firm who commenced the development of the industry. The private individuals then made some improvements to the plant, and during the year 1914 expected to carry on extensive developments. They were well under way with this work when the war broke out, but being supplied with a limited capital, they were seriously handicapped, and were compelled to close down their plant for lack of money to continue its operation. I regret to say that the plant is now in the hands of a receiver.

speechtext: I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong), b,ut I am very much interested in the statement he makes as to the result of this experiment. What would be the price of coal as compared with the price of peat for heating purposes?

speechtext:
I will give that information a little further on. As far as I can learn, this was the only real live effort on sane lines in Canada for the development of the peat industry, and after I have explained to you the enormous areas of excellent peat bogs that are available, I feel confident that you will agree with me that some decided effort should be made at the earliest possible date to develop this industry. I believe that the Government should take over this bog immediately and continue to operate it. Manufactured peat at cost should be supplied to the municipalities convenient to the bog, and since the local Government of the province of Ontario have provided means whereby a city like Ottawa could purchase this fuel, the
city should arrange for at least 5,000 tons of peat to be stored for use next winter. Other cities should be placed in a similar position. What an advantage it would have been to the people of Ottawa this winter had the corporation of this city stored
5.000	or 10,000 tons of this fuel for distribution at cost to the poorer inhabitants of the city. I sincerely hope that the Government will see to it that -a decided effort is made at the earliest possible date to place within the reach of the people in Canada an abundance of this fuel for residential and manufacturing purposes.
From the Government's development of the peat bog at Alfred, it was proven conclusively that peat could be manufactured into blocks suitable for use in industries and in private homes at an actual cost of $1.75 per ton.
