speechtext: Was that the retail price?

subtopic: PROPOSED UTILIZATION OF CANADIAN FUEL RESOURCES.
speechtext:
That was the price manufactured on the ground. Indeed, this was the actual cost of the production of the
2.000	tons of peat referred to. The railway charged one dollar per ton for its transportation to Ottawa, a distance of forty miles.
However, the peat was delivered at $5 per ton to manufacturers and householders, and from many sources I have obtained definite information sufficient to assure me that for residential purposes, in grates, in cook-stoves, in the ordinary heater, this has proved to be an ideal fuel. This is a practical demonstration of what can be accomplished, and a good reason why the Government should act. It.is true that anthracite coal has more heat units per ton, but the use of anthracite coal entails greater wastage, owing to incomplete combustion, and a larger percentage of ash. This is not necessary in the consumption of peat. Peat fuel is easily lighted, and it is not necessary to use a greater quantity than is required for cooking or heating at one time, while, on the other hand, anthracite undergoes very great wastage in this regard.
The European countries for centuries have been forced to use their natural resources. Some of these countries, which have not been richly endowed by nature with fuel resources, have been very generous in their interest towards the peat fuel industry. Large grants of money have been made annually in Sweden for the purpose of experimentation and research work, and sums of money set aside to be distributed as loans to persons desiring to engage in some phase of the peat industry. The Government of Sweden spends sixty

thousand dollars per annum in the encouragement of peat production. The Swedish Government are running their locomotives on the railways with peat powder. In Denmark, during the year 1913, 64 peat factories with 94 peat fuel plants were in operation. The demand for peat fuel in Denmark is very great.
The European war had an extraordinary effect on the peat market in Denmark. From the beginning of the war no coal has been imported, so the price of stored coal has increased all through the country. As the price went up, the demand for peat fuel developed into gigantic proportions. Dairies, brick manufactories and other manufactories started to use peat fuel, and seemed to be satisfied, in spite of the increased cost per brick for manufacture. In Russia, during the last few years, the peat fuel industry has been greatly developed. This is shown by the fact that peat fuel takes second place in the fuel consumption of the country. In 1909, 44 per cent of Russian crude oil, 33 per cent of air-dryed peat fuel, and 23 per cent of coal was used. Since then the production of peat has increased. As the cost of coal, crude oil and wood increases, the peat industry continues to develop.
The sale of machines for the manufacture of peat in Russia in the years 1912 and 1913 shows an increase of 400 per cent. It is estimated tlhat Russia is producing annually 10 million metric tons of peat fuel, out of which seven million tons are manufactured in the seven central Russian Provincial Governments. The United States, exclusive of Alaska, is estimated to have 11,200 square miles of peat bogs, averaging 9 feet in depth, and containing nearly 13,000,000,000 tons of fuel, worth, at $3 a ton, $39,000,000,000. Canada has 37,000 square miles of known peat bogs, but these form probably but a small fraction of the total, constituting a potential national asset of enormous value. The peat resources of Canada exceed those of any other country with the exception of Russia- During the period from 1908 to 1914 the Mines Branch in Canada located, mapped and investigated 140,000 acres of peat bogs in Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Manitoba, all convenient to railways and markets, estimated to be capable of yielding 115,000,000 tons of fuel and
10,500,000	tons of peat moss litter. Why do we not make use of the information obtained by our Government experts? Seven Ontario Bogs within convenient shipping 
distance of Toronto will yield 26,500,000 tons of fuel. Four bogs within a few miles of Ottawa are estimated to contain over 25,000,000 tons. Seven bogs in the Montreal district -could furnish that city with 23,500,000 tons of fuel. Five bogs along the St. Lawrence, below Quebec and convenient to that city by water, could supply 16,250,000 tons of fuel and 5,750,000 tons of peat moss litter. Nova Scotia Bogs examined in Yarmouth, Shelburne and Lunenburg counties will produce 6,250,000 tons of fuel and 500,000 tons of litter. Six bogs investigated in Prince Edward Island can furnish 1,250,000 tons of fuel and over 1,000,000 tons of litter. Seven bogs examined in Manitoba will produce 2,000,000 tons of fuel and
2,500,000	tons of litter.
Apart from the potential value of our peat bogs as a subsidiary source of fuel supply and for the production of sulphate of ammonia, there are numerous other products such as moss litter, peat dust, alcohol, acetic acid, acetone, tar, tar oils, creosote, ga9, etc., which might form the basis of paying industries, giving employment to many people, where now we have only waste lands-
As to the comparative heating value of peat fuel as delivered to the consumer, it may be said that, comparing
10 p.m. the actual heating va/lues, one ton of hard coal is equivalent to 11 tons of peat with a moisture content of 25 per cent; but, in order to arrive at a fair comparison, it is necessary to understand and carefully consider certain factors which, under certain conditions, would turn the scale in favour of peat fuel. As a fuel for cook stoves, ranges, etc., peat fuel will prove more economical than -anthracite, since, with coal, the fire must be burned continuously, and, moreover, the refuse, i. e., ash, contains a very large proportion of combustible matter.
The manufacture of sulphate of ammonia is a matter of great importance to the people of Canada. Our peat bogs in Canada are high in nitrogen, running about 2 per cent. In Italy they are running their peat bogs with a little over 1 per cent of sulphate of ammonia- Ammonium sulphate is a very valuable artificial fertilizer, for which there is a continually increasing demand in almost all parts of the world, and a ready market could be found for all the sulphate of ammonia that could be produced in Canada.
At a time like the present when stock is being taken of the natural resources of the

country, the importance of these investigations will be readily recognized. The estimated yield of 19 bogs in Ontario and Quebec, if used to produce ammonium sulphate, would give a production of 81,696,416 tons of fuel. With a production of sulphate of ammonia amounting to 4,025,525 tons which at a valuation of $65 per ton, which is a very low estimate, the value would amount to $261,659,775.
Intense agriculture has filled the granaries of the world, but fertilizers have become absolutely necessary. Soil fertility is urgently demanded. Appetite has come with eating and our demands and wants are increasing day by day. Inoculation of soil Has become an established success. Bacterized peat has been used most successfully as a medium for this purpose. Experiments in England made by Professor Bottomley, Botanical Laboratories, University of London, Kings College, as described in a book entitled " Spirit of the Soil," written by C. D. Knox, shows that treated peat gives as much as 50 to 80 times great-' er results than the best rotted stable manure, that it is free from smell, dust, weeds, disease spores and insect pests, is clean and pleasant to handle. After seven years of experiments, the American Board of Agriculture are distributing a similar preparation to farmers and recommending its use. Bacterized peat opens a field for every farmer and gardener to undertake important scientific work, in order to increase the yield from the land.
In addition to this, Dr. Eugene Haanel, the head of the Mines Branch, makes the following estimate:
that the gas available in working the large Teefleld bog for sulphate of ammonia would produce 4,000 H.P. continuously for 86 years, a total of 344,000 H.P., the total power gas available in conjunction with the utilization of all the bogs in Canada would amount to over 5,000,000 B.H.P.
Peat burns with a much smaller air supply than coal, consequently less heat is wasted than with the greater draft required to burn coal.
I believe it is the duty of this Government to take over certain peat bogs and .lignite mines and furnish the material at cost to our people. Greatly increased prices for the coming winter must be expected, and urdess some immediate action is taken, great hardships are bound to ensue. The peat bog at Alfred, Ont., is capable of immediate development, and at least 1,000 tons of peat per month could be manufactured in this bog during the summer and

fall. It is estimated that there are 3,000 interned Germans in the camps in our country; a. sufficient number of men from these camps could be employed on our peat bogs, near London, Toronto, Montreal and Quebec, to produce a supply of fuel. After the material is manufactured, it is up to the municipalities to purchase the peat and see that: it is delivered at cost to the artisan or' the farmer. The mayor of this city should have at least 5,000 tons of this material on hand for distribution during the coming winter. Similar amounts, only larger, should be stored in Toronto and Montreal, and other -cities.
In the western provinces, lignite coal should be made available for distribution to the farmers and others, and I believe that a sufficient quantity of soft coal should he brought from the mines at Sydney or thereabout, up the St. Lawrence, and distributed to the municipalities, if for no other reason than an experiment. The day may soon come when elevators will be built in Sydney harbour and boats carry coal west and wheat east.
I cannot urge too strongly on the Government the need of immediate attention to this subject. The more I investigate it, * the more convinced I am that, unless some radical steps are taken, serious suffering and hardship will be the lot of thousands of our people. During our long winter we are dependent upon artificial heat in our homes. Owing to the continual increase in the amount of fuel required for industrial purposes, and .the yearly advance in the price of fuel, I respectfully urge that the Government should tak-e over the -peat bog at Alfred at once, and also commence operations near Toronto, Montreal and Quebec, in order to establish the confidence of the people of Canada in the value of peat as a domestic and industrial fuel, and to stimulate activity in the development of our peat resources. In addition to this I respectfully urge the Government to investigate all other means of supplying our people with an abundance of fuel.
It is important that we take this matter up for the following reasons: The outlook for sufficient fuel from the United States is uncertain. We are -dependent -for a large portion of our fuel- on American resources.
It would mean the development of other profitable industries in Canada. The development of our peat bogs and other mines will furnish additional employment to Canadians in Canada.
The statistics which I have furnished have 'been gathered with greatest of care from
the departments of the Government connected with the advancement of these industries, and I submit them for the careful consideration of the Hpuse.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution moved by the member for East Lambton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong) is of considerable interest to the part of Canada from which I cpme. This House may be surprised to know that the province of Alberta has the greatest coal resources of any province in Canada; indeed, its coal resources are very much greater than those of British Columbia or Nova Scotia, the provinces whose production ranks next to that of Alberta. It is estimated in the report of the Department of Mines that Alberta's coal resources amount to 1,072,627,400,000 metric tons. If the Alberta coal mines were operating the year round, they would produce far more than would be consumed in western Canada, but owing to the various labour troubles which we have almost annually the mines do not operate regularly and the supply of coal is not such as the resources are able to furnish or even sufficient to meet the demands of the western consumers. We cannot get be-' yond Winnipeg with Alberta coal because of the competition of Pennsylvania coal. The freight rates interfere; and there is the difficulty of storing lignite coal from the prairies. If the proposed treatment of western c.oal is successful, it will make a very great difference in that respect,- but one of the great difficulties at present encountered in handling western coal is the impossibility of storing it for any great length ^ of time. The reason why the competition [DOT]of Pennsylvania coal comes so close to the supply in western Canada as Manitoba is found almost wholly in the cheap transportation rates by water.
Vessels moving the grain down the Great Lakes require traffic in return, and they offer a very cheap rate for the transportation of Pennsylvania coal to Manitoba and the head of the ilakes. It is almost impossible for those handling Alberta coal to meet that condition. It would be of great value to the labour market in the mines of the West -if there was a steady market all the year round; production would be increased, a.nd steady employment would be assured. Uncertainty of employment is one of the difficulties experienced in the mines of the West. At present we have a very serious strike in all the mines of British Columbia. I have a wire to-night from Lethbridge stating that the steam coal situ-
[>Mr. Armstrong.]
ation is extremely serious and may affect some of the railroads in western Canada because sufficient steam coal has not been stored to meet the urgent demands being made at present. We have these difficulties from time to time. If it were possible to carry out the idea that the member for East Lambton has in mind and to find a market for the coal throughout the various parts of Canada, it would be of great assist- -ance to the coal industry in western Canada and, I assume, in other parts of the Dominion as well. But I am not very confident that that can be done. The only thing that can be hoped for in connection with the domestic coal mining industry on the prairies is a rapid development of the West so that the consumption of coal will increase sufficiently to warrant the operation of more mines and the production of more coal. In my part of the country the coal mining business has not been profitable to those who have invested in it. In some cases the coal mining business has been overdone, and I do not know of any very large dividends being paid by any coal mining company in the southern part of the province of Alberta. This is due to a great extent to the lack of a steady market, of a steady demand for the coal and of an all-year-round operation of the mines. We have in Canada sufficient fuel resources to meet all our needs for years to come, if the supply could only be directed to the various parts of our own country-the coal resources of the West brought further East than at present, and those of the East brought further West. .	.
I should like to see something develop from the proposal of the member for East Lambton, but I am not very hopeful that it will toe of any 'benefit at present to the coal resources of western Canada unless some treatment can be devised which will permit the storing of the coal and enable it to be transported further away from its present source of supply.

I agree, therefore, with my hon. friend that the Government should take hold of this matter and experiment. The provincial government of Saskatchewan put in an experimental plant which has proved to a .certain extent what can be done, but that Government has not gone far enough; whoever takes hold of the business must go further and spend more money in making experiments. We have there such vast deposits of lignite that we could shut off the importation of several million dollars' worth of hard and soft coal from Pennsylvania and other eastern States and give a fuel equally as good in every respect. The fuel that is produced out of this lignite is a carbonized coal something like coke, and it will furnish as much heat to the ton as anthracite. I trust, therefore, my hon. friend who is leading the House will give this matter proper consideration and see if something cannot be done. This is an economic question for this country. Every million dollars' worth of material that we can produce in this country and that we can use in this country is a million dollars saved to the people of Canada. If this fuel is produced, those who are living in the vicinity will have this advantage that they will get the quality of fuel they want at a lower price than they are paying at the present time, because although coal is cheap in that district in its present shape it costs anyone using large quantities of it very nearly as much as to send further away and pay extra freight and get a higher quality of coal. If this lignite is going to take the place it should take, it should be put into smaller bulk so that there would be less freight and less handling. I am absolutely sure that some day not in the very distant futuTe, in the coal fields in the southwestern end of my constituency, within less than 100 miles of the province of Manitoba, there will be established plants which will use that cheap coal for generating electricity, and throughout southern Saskatchewan from Moosejaw south and throughout the southwestern corner of Manitoba electric power for lighting and cooking will be generated from that coal
We are going to get our heat from straw, I understand.

I am not posted on that, so I shall not say a word against it; it may be a good scheme. I am talking of these deposits of coal. I am sure that they could be * very easily mined, and p.ower cheaply developed by means of a generating plant. All you would have to do would be to run a shaft* into the wheel, coal it out, and dump it right into the boiler room, and one of these days that will happen. But I want to impress on the Minister of Finance and, the 'Minister of Labour that it will not happen of itself; some one must take hold of the thing arid give it a start. I trust that the Government will look into this question thoroughly and see whether the statements I have made are not perfectly justified. I have lived within a few miles of these coal fields for many, many years. I have visited them hundreds of times, and I know something about the extent of coal that is there. I am certain that if the experiments were continued a great enterprise would soon be under way and millions of money would be kept in this country that is now going to the United States in payment for coal for our well-to-do people in the cities and in the country too.

Has any estimate
been made of the quantity of coal at Este-van?

There is an estimate inthe report of the Department of Mines. The report gives the figure for the wh.ole province as 59,812,000,000 tons; the great bulk of that is on the western side of Saskatchewan, and not in the part of the country I am speaking of. I have no doubt that in this report, if I had time to look through it, I could find an estimate for this particular part of the c.ountry, but I know of my own knowledge they have been mining there for twenty or thirty years, and there are dozens of .sections that are underlaid with coal all the way from six to twelve feet thick. A twelvedoot seam gives about 12,000 tons, to the acre of saleable coal, outside altogether ol waste and what is left in the ground, and I do not think there has been a square mile of coal mined in all that territory yet; we are taking up only from three to four hundred thousand tons a year. There is coal enough there to last as long as our grandchildren; the extent of it has never been gauged. A farmer

twenty miles beyond the supposed limits of the coal area will very often strike a seam from six to ten feet thick if he goes down 300 feet. West of Estevan are what were formerly called the Dirt Hills, which were not supposed to be good from an agricultural point of view, but which are now settled and growing good crops of wheat, and which contain considerable deposits of coal. In the country south of Moosejaw there are outcroppings of coal right along, and the settlers dig the coal up and keep themselves in fuel all the year round. This applies to the whole country south of Regina, but more particularly to that country about forty miles south of Moosejaw. Then, again, about 200 miles west of the Estevan [DOT]oal fields there are out-croppings of coal near the Wood Mountain. In fact, there is coal practically all through the southern portion of the province. In the western part of the province the quality of lignite is better, and is called by some people Galt coal. At Taber there are huge deposits, and also at Medicine Hat, where they' mined coal in the old days twenty-five years ago. So my hon. friend need not -worry about the extent of the coal deposits. The coal is there, and is only awaiting the hand of man to dig it up. If these deposits were in Germany, or France, or any other of the thickly populated countries of Europe a fine fuel would soon be made out of this lignite, which is about the poorest quality we have in the West, and they would be able to make enough out of the by-products alone to pay for the expense of mining. All I ask is that the Government look into this matter thoroughly, and I am sure that if they will continue the experiments they will see that the enterprise is well worth going into.

Most of the discussion that has taken place so far on this resolution has been with regard to lignite. My hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) has raised another matter which I wish to discuss for a few moments, and that is the use of straw for fuel. It must appeal to any one who has been through western Canada and seen the great quantities of straw that are burned on our farms during the fall season, what a tremendous waste is going on of material which could be devoted to some economic purpose. Straw is of no value as a fertilizer, and various experiments have been made with a view to its utilization either as a fuel or in some other manner. My attention was directed especially to it a
couple of months ago when I was in Moosejaw with Mr. Knowles, a member of this House, also Mr. George W. Brown, formerly Lieutenant Governor of the province, and Professor R. D. McLaurin of Saskatoon University. We visited a machine shop where experiments were being conducted by a Mr. Harrison, who is the inventor of a process for extracting gas from straw. The method is by means of a retort in which the straw is placed, and, under heat the gas is driven out into a receptacle called a scrubber, which contains water and iron filings. There the gas is cleansed, and then it passes into a gasometer. In the process of passing through the scrubber a tar is given off which runs, I understand, some ten gallons to the ton, and which is black in colour and heavy in composition. It contains the elements of coal-tar, and is consequently useful in the manufacture of by-products of coal-tar. While any straw may be used in this process, it is said that flax straw gives the best results. I saw cooking being done, stoves heated, and gas engines run by means of this gas. The gas is a blue flame, and a mantle is used for lighting. Apparently it is a very pure gas, f.or after being under a vessel for some time very little carbon is shown. It is estimated that twenty tons of straw a year would light and furnish heat for cooking for a seven-roomed farm house. I am told that one hundred tons a year would provide all the heat, light and power that would be used about an ordinary farm. Mr. Harrison said to me that he could use a tank of the same size as a gasolene tank of a Ford car and, by compressing the gas in it, could carry enough gas to run a Ford ear for 100 miles. If that would work out, it pretty well solves the power problem in the West. When one bears in mind that straw runs about two tons to the acre, it is easy to see what tremendous quantities are available, what practically unlimited quantities are in the possession of every farmer.
The apparatus to which I have referred is very simple in construction. I do not know that it is yet being manufactured for sale. Fortunately it can be used in small plants, and so individual farmers may have it, and I have every reason to believe that for less than $1,000 it can be installed, covered and ready for use. speechtext:
The question raised by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong) is a very important one particularly to the part of the country from which I come. The most practical problem involved is the opening of the ways of transportation between the far East of Canada and the West. In the East we have coal in abundance, and other commodities also that are required in the West, while Ontario and the West has abundance of things that we need. To make possible the exchange of these commodities is the problem. Of course, this is not a new question with myself, coming as I do from the coal fields of Nova Scotia and having realized long ago the importance of being able to send our coal, our lumber, and other products, into Ontario and the West in competition with the United States and other places which may seek the same markets.
It would seem that the deepening of our waterways is the true solution of the question. If steamers can be loaded at Port Arthur for Atlantic ports or any ports intervening, and, reversely, steamers can be loaded at Atlantic ports for the trip up the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes to Port Arthur and intervening ports, the problem will be solved. I submit to the Minister of Finance and the Government that nothing more deserves their attention than the deepening of our waterways. I submit that the construction of the Hudson Bay Railway or the Georgian Bay canal should not be considered in comparison with the practical question of deepening the canals of the St. Lawrence. Jf it were passible for us to load coal in Sydney fox Port Arthur and intervening ports, we should be in a position to give to the people of Ontario excellent fuel for all purposes. It has been, represented by some that Nova Scotia coal is not a good coal for domestic purposes. I can assure hon. members-and many people in the Maritime Provinces can bear me
[Mr McCraney.]
out-that it is a very excellent article for domestic purposes. And if it is necessary to convert it into coke, it has proven its worth in that way; we have large steel works in Nova Scotia deDending altogether on coke from our own coal. If facilities were placed at the command of our people we should be able to land our coal, our iron, our steel, our coke, as well as tar and chemicals produced from coal, our potatoes, lumber, and other articles which we have in abundance, in Ontario ports, and even send them to .points in the West. In return, we would take from Ontario flour, wheat, corn, bacon, and manufactured goods, and from the West the products that they have in abundance there. The use of oux coal would afford cheap power for the manufactories of Ontario. On the other hand, we would be able to lay down in these sections cheap coal of a most excellent quality. Instead of thinking about storing wheat in elevators on Hudson Bay, if you deepened the canals and opened up a way from Port Arthur to Atlantic ports, such as Halifax, North Sydney and Louisburg, your elevators would be built at Halifax, North Sydney and Louisburg, where you have the open ocean without a speck of ice to interfere with you all the year round. You can store your wheat there and you are not under the necessity of having your wheat in elevators at Port Arthur, Montreal and other places for the greater part of the year ice hound. The ships that would bring up coal, lumber and other articles as well would carry wheat back and a profitable trade would be established through the Great Lakes. Store the coal for winter purposes in convenient places in the West. There is no trouble in your erecting elevated chutes or pockets by erecting trestles over railways and alongside of wharves from where you discharge your coal, so that your cars would run under these chutes at any time in the winter and it would toe easy to handle the coal. That is the way they store coal in chutes at the great coal centres of Nova Scotia. The -coal is ready in two or two and a half hours to load the largest ship that comes alongside the pier. In like manner you could store coal at central places in the West, and your coal cars could run under these chutes and get the coal. You have the opportunity of storing your wheat on the Atlantic coast and storing your coal at whatever places in the West may toe found convenient toy this interchange of traffic once the canals are deepened. I may be talking without knowledge. I have no great knowledge of what is necessary to deepen these

canals, but we do know that they are now down to a depth of 14 feet. It is expected that the Welland canal will soon be down to a depth of 25 feet, and if that can be done on the Welland canal, and if they have been able to go to a depth of 14 feet on the various other ' canals, there is no reason why they should not be brought down to the proper depth. It would be a magnificent boon to the country and something that would redound to the general advantage of all Canada.
We have a supply of coal, iron and steel in Nova Scotia which is inexhaustible, and there need be no fear that great expense will be put on the canals and that the facilities will not be profitable because we have not a sufficient supply. I do not know that it is any exaggeration to state that the coal belt of Nova Scotia is 250 miles 'long, extending from Louisburg, on the Atlantic, away down around the sinuosities of the Gulf of St. Lawrence to Cumberland, about 250 miles of coast, averaging between 10 and 25 miles wide. That magnificent belt of coal has only really been touched here and there although millions of tons are being taken out of it. With these great opportunities for the development of coal, iron and steel, lumber and other forest products and with the capabilities of Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia in the production of root crops that would be available to our friends in the West, a magnificent opportunity would be established for a permanent and profitable trade within our own bounds, making us forever independent practically of anybody outside of Canada. I felt that it was incumbent upon me, in view of the great interest that is taken in. this matter by the people living in the part of the country from which I come, to make these observations. I feel under a debt of gratitude to my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) for having brought this 'very practical and important subject before the House and the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry my hon.
friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) is not present this evening because it had been his intention to speak on this resolution. I join in the expression of gratitude ef the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. McKenzie) towards the mover of this resolution, the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) for his very able exposition of the subject and for the painstaking attention that he has evidently bestowed on the
preparation of the speech in which he has brought it to the attention of the House. I followed his remarks with the closest attention and all who have spoken are unanimous in their view as to the extreme importance of the question of the fuel supply of the Dominion. My hon. friend from East Lambton has truly pointed out that our supplies of bituminous and anthracite coal-or more properly bituminous coal, because we have comparatively little anthracite developed-lie on.the extreme east and west and that, in so far as the central provinces are concerned, Quebec and Ontario are largely dependent for their c.oal supply upon the United States to the south. The province of Ontario is dependent at the present time for the bituminous coal -supply used in connection with its great industries upon the United States. The hon. member for East Lambton has pointed out that this is a -situation which might at some time give rise to apprehension. In that connection I might mention the great importance to the province of Ontario of the development of her unexcelled water powers. These water powers, I think, will play an increasingly important part in the economy of Ontario and Quebec and of other provinces as weE in the future, and in the electrical development of the country as applied to production. I think that Canada has the greatest resources in water powers of any country in the world, and certainly the future will witness a very great development in that connection. The hon. member for North Cape Breton has pointed out the great resources of Nova Scotia and Cape Breton Island in coal. He has stated, and I think truly, that their resources in that respect are practically inexhaustible. In Nova Scotia, and especially in Cape Breton Island, there are available for the production of coke and steel all the natural elements required comprising the iron ore which is procured from Belle Isle, limestone in practically unlimited quantities, as well as immense resources in coal, the coal areas extending out underneath the sea. So that, so far as Nova Scotia herself is concerned, her industrial future would seem to be assured. But there is coal there in amounts more than adequate for even her increasing industrial requirements, and my hon. friend to-night has expressed the opinion that if the St. Lawrence canals were deepened that coal might be made available for the requirements of central -and western Canada. I think there is a great deal to he said for that view. The

deepening of the Welland canal had been proceeding apace before the outbreak of the war, and I have no doubt that upon the conclusion of the war, as soon as it is financially practicable to resume work, the deepening of that canal will be completed-And I should look forward myself to the deepening also of the St. Lawrence canals, as my hon. friend has suggested. I think that is bound to come in the development of -Canada. The war naturally interrupted many of these projects which had engaged our attention before its outbreak. How long it will last, of course, we do not know, or how much expense it will entail upon the country. Until we do know that it is premature to express an opinion as to the undertaking of these large works, no doubt of national importance, all of them, which engaged the attention of this and preceding 'Governments in the past, and will undoubtedly engage the attention of Governments in the future, after the war is over.
The question of the development of our peat resources has been touched upon. There is no doubt that these resources are vast. I have no practical knowledge as to peat, but so far as my experience has gone, up to date its commercial development does not appear to have been practicable. The industry has always appeared promising, and yet when capital has been invested in it, with the outlook, so far as one could judge most favourable, conditions have arisen under which success has not been possible, and money has been lost. The result is that, so far as Ontario is concerned, the peat industry has not attained any considerable dimensions or its development met with any considerable degree of success, at least that is my impression. But while that is so, it by no means follows that the future development of the peat industry is destined t.o such a fate. It is quite possible that, with the progress of 11 p.m. invention and with the increase in population, peat may play a large part in our future domestic and industrial economy. I think that very probable. So far as the West is concerned, it has been pointed out by the hon. member for Assinib.oia (Mr. Turriff) to-night that the coal or lignite areas there are practically inexhaustible. I think that is so. In Saskatchewan and Alberta we know there are many deposits of coal and lignite. The difficulty, it appears to me, at the present time, is that you have a comparatively sparse population, and as success in mining coal of that character will depend on 
demand and demand immediately at hand, because transporati.on difficulties have to to be taken into consideration, notwithstanding the best efforts that might be put forth, the development of the fuel areas of Saskatchewan and Alberta as well as the southern part of Manitoba must proceed rather slowly. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) has pointed out another reason which inclines me to the same view. So far as British Columbia is concerned, we have got the bituminous c.oal there from which is produced the coke which is indispensable in connection with the industries of southern British Columbia. All these considerations indicate the extreme importance of the question of c.oal and other fuel for the industrial development of Canada. Of almost as great importance, though not quite as great, is the question of the supply and cheapness of fuel, soft and hard coal, and lignite if it can be made available, for domestic use. The question will 'probably become more acute as the population of the country increases, and I myself would hope to see, apart from any action of the Government, a progressive demand for fuel, such as soft coal and lignite, for these purposes. But my hon. friend is right in urging that the Government should give special attention to the whole question, because it touches vitally our production and the comfort of our people, -and is therefore one of the larger problems of Canada.
So far as I can see, the resolution is one which might well be adopted by the House. I shall make it a point to bring it to the attention of the Minister of Mines and the. department under him. I would suggest to the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) that the resolution be amended to read instead of "through legislation and otherwise," "through legislation or otherwise." It has not been shown that legislation is necessaray in this connection. Of course, if any legislation is necessary, the Government could bring it down. If the hon. member will make that slight change, I think that, so far as the Government is concerned, the resolution may be accepted. We are all as one as to the extreme importance of the matter, and while the energies of the Government must necessarily be engrossed by the war, still I see no reason why the department should not go carefully into the matter, and if there is anything which the Government can do at the present time, we shall be only too glad to do it.

I appreciate the generous treatment which the House has

given this resolution, and I appreciate also the words of the hon. member for St. John city. He has called attention to the development of electricity in Canada. I do not think that he was present when I was referring to that subject. I called attention to the fact that were it not for the present development of electricity in Canada, we should be compelled to import from the United States and other outside points an amount of coal equal to the amount which we are importing to-day, and I urged the Government to see if it was possible to find other means of developing electrical energy in Canada. What I am particularly urging on the Government is the need of investigating the fuel resources of Canada; that steps should be taken to see whether the available fuel supply-electricity and oil shales included, if you like-in our country can be developed along scientific and practical lines, in order that our people may be able to secure fuel at a more reasonable rate than that at which- they are now securing it. I feel that we should dispose of the resolution to-night, because the days are going by when private members have the opportunity of taking up such resolutions. If the Finance Minister would agree to have the resolution include electrical energy and oil shales, I have no objection whatever. I call attention to the fact that we have a commission appointed for scientific research, composed of a number of prominent men from the different universities, including Professor MacCallum, who is at its head. It would be their duty, I think, to take this matter up and see if they could develop it along practical, rational and common sense lines.
